passages.text:
What, then, must be done except this? I will travel to Egypt, befriend the hierophants and prophets of the inner sanctuaries, and, after seeking and finding a magician, persuade him with a large sum of money to perform a sending up of a soul—the practice called necromancy—while I make an inquiry as though about some particular matter. But the inquiry will be about learning whether the soul is immortal. I will know the soul’s answer—that it is immortal—not because it has spoken or I have even heard it, but merely because it has appeared, so that, having seen it with my own eyes, I may have a self-sufficient and adequate conclusion from its mere appearance that it exists. The obscure words that belong to hearing will then no longer be able to overturn the eyes’ own evidence.

Nevertheless, I put this very plan before a philosopher of my acquaintance, who advised me in many ways not to dare it. “For if the soul does not heed the magician,” he said, “you will have acted against the laws that forbid people to do such things, and you will live with a guilty conscience. But if it does heed him, then, besides your living with a guilty conscience, I think you will no longer make progress in piety, for whose sake you even dared this. For they say that the divine is hostile toward those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies.” When I heard this, I became more hesitant to undertake such a thing, but I did not abandon my original intention. Instead, I grew despondent, as though my impulse had been obstructed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a sending up of a soul—the practice called necromancy
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Sending up” preserves the directional image of ἀναπομπή rather than replacing it with the broader “summoning”; the parenthetical identification is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ λαλῆσαι ἢ καὶ ἀκοῦσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not because it has spoken or I have even heard it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitives do not state their subjects. Context supports the soul as speaker and Clement as hearer; the more impersonal “not from speaking or even hearing” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a self-sufficient and adequate conclusion
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἀπόφασις denotes a determination or conclusion, not the unrelated sense “denial.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια τὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ἀνατρέψαι ἄδηλα ῥήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: The obscure words that belong to hearing will then no longer be able to overturn the eyes’ own evidence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The obscure words are the grammatical agent, and what belongs to the eyes is the object. “Evidence” makes the substantival τὰ … ἴδια intelligible without changing the contrast between sight and hearing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will live with a guilty conscience
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb denotes living with a bad or troubled conscience, not merely living unhappily.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων σκύλλουσιν τὰς ψυχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῇ λύσει is read temporally or circumstantially, without making the harassers the explicit agents of the dissolution. “Through the dissolution of dead bodies” is a viable instrumental alternative. Reading λύσις as the release of souls from bodies is possible in context, but the supplied construction does not itself explicitly say that the necromancers release them.

passages.text: And, so that I may not recount such matters to you at great length, while I was occupied with so many reflections and circumstances, a certain report arose quietly during the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Beginning at the spring equinox, it continually grew and, truly a good messenger of God, ran throughout the world, unable to keep silent and conceal God’s will. It therefore became more widespread and greater each time, saying that a certain man in Judea, having begun at the spring equinox, was announcing to the Jews the good news of the kingdom of the everlasting God. He said that any one of them would enjoy it if he first set his way of life right. And to secure belief in him—that he did these things while full of divinity—he performed many marvelous signs and wonders by command alone, as one who had received authority from God. For he made the deaf hear and the blind see again; he made those with deformed limbs walk and set the lame upright; he drove away every disease and put every demon to flight. Even people with leprosy or scabies were healed and went away merely by fixing their gaze on him from a distance. Dead people brought to him were raised, and there was nothing he was unable to do. Indeed, the further time advanced, the far greater and more firmly established became—not the report any longer, I mean, but the truth of the matter—because of the increasing number of visitors. Assemblies were already forming in various places for deliberation and inquiry into who the one who had appeared might be and what he meant to say.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the spring equinox
lexical_decisions.rationale: τροπή can denote a seasonal turning point, including an equinox. “At the turn of spring” is a less technically specific alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος διέτρεχε τὸν κόσμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: truly a good messenger of God, ran throughout the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς ἀληθῶς is taken idiomatically as “truly” or “in truth,” affirming the report’s personification rather than introducing a comparison. ἄγγελος retains the ordinary sense “messenger”; “angel of God” is lexically possible but would make the personification more specifically supernatural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: first set his way of life right
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here concerns conduct or manner of life, while προ- supplies the prior action required before enjoying the kingdom.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ δὲ πιστεύεσθαι αὐτὸν χάριν ὅτι θειότητος γέμων ταῦτα ποιεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to secure belief in him—that he did these things while full of divinity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ὅτι clause is treated as the content to be believed. It can alternatively be read causally: “to secure belief in him, because he does these things while full of divinity.” “Full of divine power” is a possible contextual rendering of θειότης, but “divinity” preserves the source’s stronger wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he made those with deformed limbs walk and set the lame upright
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the source’s distinction between κυλλοί, people with bent or deformed limbs, and χωλοί, the lame.

lexical_decisions.chosen: people with leprosy or scabies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering reads the juxtaposed adjectives as two groups within the surrounding enumeration of afflictions: λεπροί as people with leprosy and ψωροί as people with a scabby or mangy skin condition, here rendered “scabies.” Because there is no conjunction, the words can alternatively describe one group as both leprous and scabby: “scabby leprous people.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the increasing number of visitors
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω describes people visiting or sojourning in a place. “Through more of those arriving” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Assemblies … in various places
lexical_decisions.rationale: συστήματα can denote organized groups, gatherings, or assemblies; the following deliberation and inquiry favor “assemblies.”

source_issues.issue: The printed full stop interrupts the article and its dependent genitive, where it cannot function as normal sentence punctuation. The translation provisionally treats it as intrusive editorial punctuation while preserving all the printed words.

passages.text:
And indeed, once in that very year, at the autumn equinox, someone stood up publicly and shouted, saying, “Men of Rome, listen! The Son of God is present in Judea, promising eternal life to all who desire it, if they live according to the intention of the Father who sent him. Therefore change your way—from worse things to better, from temporary things to eternal. Recognize that there is one God, the heavenly one, whose world you inhabit unjustly before his righteous eyes. But if you make this change and live according to his will, you will be carried into another age, become everlasting, and enjoy his ineffable good things. If, however, you disobey, your souls will be cast, after the dissolution of the body, into the place of fire, where, while being punished eternally, they will reorient themselves to no avail. For each person’s present life is the time for reorientation.”

As I listened to this, I was distressed that no one from among such great crowds, after hearing so momentous an announcement, had said, “I will travel to Judea so that I may see whether this man is telling the truth when he says these things.” For the claim was that the Son of God had come to Judea and, for the sake of a good and eternal hope, was revealing the will of the Father who sent him—especially since what they say he proclaims is no small matter. For he confidently affirms that the souls of some, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, while the souls of others, cast into unquenchable fire, will be punished throughout the age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in that very year
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase locates the event at or close upon the same year. “About that same year” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the autumn equinox
lexical_decisions.rationale: As with the corresponding spring expression, τροπή denotes a seasonal turning point; “at the turn of autumn” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: change your way
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording calls for a change in manner or way of life. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω word group later in the passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν· ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: they will reorient themselves to no avail. For … the time for reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The cognate verb and noun are rendered consistently under the supplied terminology policy. “They will repent uselessly … the time for repentance” is the traditional alternative; “they will regret it to no avail” would emphasize their futile response under punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his ineffable good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόρρητος can mean secret, forbidden to disclose, or unutterable. “Ineffable” fits the transcendent benefits here while preserving their unspeakable character.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the claim was that the Son of God had come to Judea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς ὅτι can introduce reported content or give a causal explanation. The context of a public report favors reported content; “since indeed the Son of God had come” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the phrase is anarthrous here, it refers contextually to the previously identified ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱός. “A son of God” remains grammatically possible if the phrase is read indefinitely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will be punished throughout the age
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the explicit noun αἰών rather than automatically assimilating it to the nearby ἀϊδίως. In this context “will be punished forever” is also semantically supportable.

source_issues.issue: The printed middle dot falls inside the article-genitive-noun phrase and interrupts “the dissolution of the body.” The translation provisionally treats it as intrusive editorial punctuation.

passages.text: While saying these things about others, I also spoke to myself: “Why do I blame others when I am under the same charge of negligence? No, I will set out for Judea after first arranging my own affairs.” Yet although I had resolved on this course, a long period of delay followed, because the affairs of life were difficult to disentangle. At last, then, I somehow reflected on the nature of life: by entangling those who are eager in hope, it lies in wait for them. Moreover, I reflected on how long I had been stealthily drawn in while being tossed about by hopes, and on the fact that we human beings die while occupied in this way. Leaving all my affairs just as they happened to be, I hurried to Portus. After reaching the harbor and putting out to sea, I was carried by the winds’ hostility to Alexandria instead of Judea. Held there for lack of winds, I spent time with the philosophers and recounted the accounts concerning both the report and the man who had appeared in Rome. They replied, “We do not know the man who appeared in Rome. But about the one who had been in Judea and whom the report calls the Son of God, we have also heard from many who have come from there as well, and we have learned about all the wonders he performed by speaking.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after first arranging my own affairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: διατίθημι with βίος can refer to putting one’s life in order. The following practical delays favor arranging personal affairs rather than an exclusively moral sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I somehow reflected on the nature of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡδίποτε is taken adverbially as “somehow or other.” The unusual expression is intelligible without conjectural alteration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by entangling those who are eager in hope, it lies in wait for them
lexical_decisions.rationale: Life remains the implied subject of both participle and verb. “Those who hurry” is the more literal alternative for τοὺς σπεύδοντας.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: how long I had been stealthily drawn in while being tossed about by hopes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative ὃν … χρόνον is read as duration and represented by “how long,” rather than as the direct object of εἰσεκλάπην. The verb is given its inward and surreptitious force as “had been stealthily drawn in.” “Had slipped in unnoticed” is possible if the passive form is understood intransitively, while “had been inveigled” is another contextual possibility; the destination or situation entered is not expressed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Portus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The capitalized Πόρτον is treated as Portus, Rome’s harbor settlement, rather than translated generically as “to the port.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the winds’ hostility
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the source’s personifying image rather than reducing the phrase to “because of adverse winds.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῆς φήμης καὶ τοῦ ἐν Ῥώμῃ φανέντος ἔλεγον τοὺς λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: recounted the accounts concerning both the report and the man who had appeared in Rome
lexical_decisions.rationale: The syntax is somewhat redundant, but λόγους can denote accounts concerning both topics. “Related what the report said and the words of the man” is possible, though it more strongly makes the second genitive possessive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ γενομένου καὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης λεγομένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who had been in Judea and whom the report calls the Son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης explicitly identifies the report as the source of the designation “Son of God.” The broader γενομένου is rendered neutrally as “had been”; “had appeared” or “had emerged” is possible in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ παρὰ πολλῶν τῶν κἀκεῖθεν ἐληλυθότων ἠκούσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we have also heard from many who have come from there as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: The additive wording is retained without supplying an unexpressed first source for ἠκούσαμεν. That first point of comparison could be Clement’s account or another source; ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης belongs explicitly to the preceding designation, not necessarily to the verb “we have heard.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wonders he performed by speaking
lexical_decisions.rationale: The circumstantial participle λαλῶν can express means, yielding miracles performed by speech. “The wonders he performed while speaking” is also grammatically possible.

source_issues.source_quote: οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop separates καί from the following relative construction, leaving the latter as an abrupt fragment. The translation provisionally treats the stop as intrusive editorial punctuation while retaining the difficult wording that follows.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃν ποτε

source_issues.source_quote: ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος
source_issues.issue: The supplied wording is lexically and syntactically unusual but is retained unchanged. The translation provisionally reads χρόνον as an accusative of duration and εἰσεκλάπην with passive inward or surreptitious-entry force. An intransitive understanding such as “had slipped in unnoticed” remains possible; no conjectural correction is proposed.

passages.source_text: τί οὖν χρὴ ποιεῖν ἢ τοῦτο; εἰς Αἴγυπτον πορεύσομαι καὶ τοῖς τῶν ἀδύτων ἱεροφάνταις τε καὶ προφήταις φιλιωθήσομαι καὶ μάγον ζητήσας καὶ εὑρὼν χρήμασι πολλοῖς πείσω, ὅπως ψυχῆς ἀναπομπὴν (τὴν λεγομένην νεκρομαντείαν) ποιήσῃ, ἐμοῦ ὡς περὶ πράγματός τινος πυνθανομένου· ἡ δὲ πεῦσις ἔσται περὶ τοῦ μαθεῖν εἰ ἀθάνατος ἡ ψυχή. ἡ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπόκρισις ὅτι ἀθάνατός ἐστιν, οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ λαλῆσαι ἢ καὶ ἀκοῦσαι ἔσται μοι γνῶναι, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τοῦ ὀφθῆναι μόνον, ἵνα αὐτοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἰδὼν αὐτὴν αὐτάρκη καὶ ἱκανὴν ἀπόφασιν ἔχω ἐκ τοῦ μόνον φανῆναι ὅτι ἔστιν· καὶ οὐκέτι δυνήσεται τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια τὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ἀνατρέψαι ἄδηλα ῥήματα. ὅμως καὶ αὐτὴν ταύτην τὴν σκέψιν ἀντέβαλλόν τινι συνήθει φιλοσόφῳ, ὃς συνεβούλευσέν μοι τοῦτο μὴ τολμᾶν κατὰ πολλοὺς τρόπους. εἴτε γὰρ οὐκ εἰσακούσεται (φησίν) ἡ ψυχὴ τῷ μάγῳ, σὺ τοῖς ταῦτα ποιεῖν ἀπαγορεύουσι νόμοις ὡς ἀντιπράξας δυσσυνειδήτως βιώσεις· εἰ δὲ ἐπακούσεται, μετὰ τοῦ δυσσυνειδήτως σε βιοῦν οἶμαι τὰ τῆς εὐσεβείας σοι μηκέτι προχωρεῖν, οὗ εἵνεκεν καὶ ἐτόλμησας· ἐχθραίνειν γὰρ τὸ θεῖον λέγουσιν ἐπὶ τοῖς τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων σκύλλουσιν τὰς ψυχάς. ἐγὼ δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούσας ὀκνηρότερος μὲν πρὸς τὸ τοιοῦτον ἐγχειρῆσαι ἐγενόμην, τῆς δὲ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς μου οὐκ ἐπαυσάμην βουλῆς, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐμποδισθεὶς τὴν ὁρμὴν ἠθύμουν.

καὶ ἵνα μή σοι τὰ τοιαῦτα μακρῷ διηγήσωμαι λόγῳ, ἐν τοσούτοις λογισμοῖς καὶ πράγμασιν ὄντος μου φήμη τις ἠρέμα ἐπὶ τῆς Τιβερίου Καίσαρος βασιλείας ἐξ ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς τὴν ἀρχὴν λαμβάνουσα ηὔξανεν ἑκάστοτε καὶ ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος διέτρεχε τὸν κόσμον, τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ βούλημα σιγᾶν στέγειν μὴ δυναμένη. ἑκάστοτε οὖν πλείων καὶ μείζων ἐγίνετο, λέγουσα ὥς τις ποτὲ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ, ἐξ ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς λαβὼν τὴν ἀρχήν, Ἰουδαίοις τὴν. τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ εὐαγγελίζεται βασιλείαν, ἧς ἀπολαύειν λέγει ἐάν τις αὐτῶν προκατορθώσῃ τὴν πολιτείαν· τοῦ δὲ πιστεύεσθαι αὐτὸν χάριν ὅτι θειότητος γέμων ταῦτα ποιεῖ, πολλὰ θαυμάσια σημεῖά τε καὶ τέρατα διαπράττεται κελεύσει μόνῃ, ὡς παρὰ θεοῦ εἰληφὼς τὴν ἐξουσίαν· κωφοὺς γὰρ ποιεῖ ἀκούειν, τυφλοὺς ἀναβλέπειν, κυλλοὺς ποιεῖ περιπατεῖν, χωλοὺς ἀνορθοῖ, πᾶσαν νόσον ἀπελαύνει, πάντα δαίμονα φυγαδεύει. ἀλλὰ καὶ λεπροὶ ψωροὶ ἐκ διαστήματος μόνον ἐνορῶντες αὐτῷ ἰώμενοι ἀπαλλάσσονται. νεκροὶ δὲ προσφερόμενοι ἐγείρονται, καὶ οὐδέν ἐστιν ὃ ἀδυνατεῖ ποιεῖν. καὶ ὅσῳ γε μᾶλλον ὁ χρόνος προέκοπτεν, πολὺ μείζων διὰ πλειόνων τῶν ἐπιδημούντων βεβαιοτέρα ἐγίνετο οὐκέτι φήμη λέγω, ἀλλὰ τοῦ πράγματος ἡ ἀλήθεια· ἤδη γάρ ποτε καὶ συστήματα κατὰ τόπους ἐγίνετο βουλῆς καὶ σκέψεως, τὸ τίς ἂν εἴη ὁ φανεὶς καὶ τί βούλεται λέγειν.

καὶ δὴ ποτέ τις πρὸς αὐτῷ τῷ ἔτει ἐν φθινοπωρινῇ τροπῇ δημοσία στὰς ἐβόα λέγων Ἄνδρες Ῥωμαῖοι, ἀκούσατε· ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱὸς ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ πάρεστιν, ἐπαγγελλόμενος πᾶσιν τοῖς βουλομένοις ζωὴν αἰώνιον, ἐὰν τὰ κατὰ γνώμην τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτὸν πατρὸς βιώσωσιν. διὸ μεταβάλλεσθε τὸν τρόπον ἀπὸ τῶν χειρόνων ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα, ἀπὸ τῶν προσκαίρων ἐπὶ τὰ αἰώνια· γνῶτε ἕνα θεὸν εἶναι τὸν ἐπουράνιον, οὗ τὸν κόσμον ἀδίκως οἰκεῖτε ἔμπροσθεν τῶν αὐτοῦ δικαίων ὀφθαλμῶν. ἀλλ’ ἐὰν μεταβάλησθε καὶ κατὰ τὴν αὐτοῦ βούλησιν βιώσητε, εἰς ἕτερον αἰῶνα ἐνεχθέντες καὶ ἀΐδιοι γινόμενοι τῶν ἀπορρήτων αὐτοῦ ἀγαθῶν ἀπολαύσετε· ἐὰν δὲ ἀπειθήσητε, αἱ ψυχαὶ ὑμῶν μετὰ τὴν τοῦ σώματος·λύσιν εἰς τὸν τόπον τοῦ πυρὸς βληθήσονται, ὅπου ἀϊδίως κολαζόμεναι ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν· ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς ἡ νῦν ἑκάστου ζωὴ τυγχάνει. ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν ταῦτα ἀκούων ἠχθόμην ὅτι οὐδεὶς ἐκ τοσούτων ὄχλων τηλικαύτην ἀγγελίαν ἀκούσας εἴρηκεν Εἰς Ἰουδαίαν πορεύσομαι, ἵνα ἴδω εἰ ταῦθ’ οὗτος λέγων ἀληθεύει. ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ, ἀγαθῆς καὶ αἰωνίας ἐλπίδος χάριν τὴν τοῦ ἀποστείλαντος πατρὸς βούλησιν ἐκφαίνων, ἐπεὶ καὶ ὅπερ λέγουσιν αὐτὸν κηρύσσειν, οὐκ ἔστιν μικρόν· ὧν μὲν γὰρ τὰς ψυχὰς διαβεβαιοῦται αἰωνίους οὔσας αἰωνίων ἀπολαύσειν ἀγαθῶν, ὧν δὲ ἐν πυρὶ ἀσβέστῳ ῥιφείσας τὸν αἰῶνα κολασθήσεσθαι.

ταῦτ’ ἐγὼ λέγων περὶ ἄλλων καὶ ἐμαυτῷ ὡμίλησα λέγων Τί ἄλλους μέμφομαι, ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ τῆς ἀμελείας ὑπάρχων ἐγκλήματι; ἀλλ’ εἰς Ἰουδαίαν ὁρμήσω, πρότερον τὸν ἐμὸν διαθεὶς βίον. καὶ δὴ οὕτως βουλευσαμένου μου πολὺς ὁ τῆς παρολκῆς ἐγενήθη χρόνος, τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων δυσεκλύτων ὄντων. πέρας γοῦν συννοήσας ὡδίποτε τὴν τοῦ βίου φύσιν ὅτι ἐλπίδι ἐμπλέκων τοὺς σπεύδοντας ἐνεδρεύει, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος, καὶ ὅτι οὕτως ἀσχολούμενοι οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἀποθνῄσκομεν, τὰ πάντα μου ὡς ἔτυχεν ἀφεὶς εἰς Πόρτον ὥρμησα, καὶ εἰς λιμένα ἐλθὼν καὶ ἀναχθεὶς ἀνέμων ἔχθραις ἀντὶ τοῦ εἰς Ἰουδαίαν εἰς Ἀλεξάνδρειαν ἠνέχθην. καὶ ἀνέμων ἀπορίᾳ ἐπισχεθεὶς ἐκεῖ συνεφοίτων τοῖς φιλοσόφοις καὶ τὰ τῆς φήμης καὶ τοῦ ἐν Ῥώμῃ φανέντος ἔλεγον τοὺς λόγους. οἱ δ᾽ ἀπεκρίναντο ὅτι τὸν μὲν ἐν Ῥώμῃ φανέντα οὐκ ἴσμεν, περὶ δὲ τοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ γενομένου καὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης λεγομένου καὶ παρὰ πολλῶν τῶν κἀκεῖθεν ἐληλυθότων ἠκούσαμεν καὶ περὶ πάντων ὧν λαλῶν ἐποίει θαυμασίων ἐμάθομεν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text:
What, then, must be done except this? I will travel to Egypt, befriend the hierophants and prophets of the inner sanctuaries, and, after seeking and finding a magician, persuade him with a large sum of money to perform a sending up of a soul—the practice called necromancy—while I make an inquiry as though about some particular matter. But the inquiry will be about learning whether the soul is immortal. I will know the soul’s answer—that it is immortal—not because it has spoken or I have even heard it, but merely because it has appeared, so that, having seen it with my own eyes, I may have a self-sufficient and adequate conclusion from its mere appearance that it exists. The obscure words that belong to hearing will then no longer be able to overturn the eyes’ own evidence.

Nevertheless, I put this very plan before a philosopher of my acquaintance, who advised me in many ways not to dare it. “For if the soul does not heed the magician,” he said, “you will have acted against the laws that forbid people to do such things, and you will live with a guilty conscience. But if it does heed him, then, besides your living with a guilty conscience, I think you will no longer make progress in piety, for whose sake you even dared this. For they say that the divine is hostile toward those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies.” When I heard this, I became more hesitant to undertake such a thing, but I did not abandon my original intention. Instead, I grew despondent, as though my impulse had been obstructed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a sending up of a soul—the practice called necromancy
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Sending up” preserves the directional image of ἀναπομπή rather than replacing it with the broader “summoning”; the parenthetical identification is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ λαλῆσαι ἢ καὶ ἀκοῦσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not because it has spoken or I have even heard it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitives do not state their subjects. Context supports the soul as speaker and Clement as hearer; the more impersonal “not from speaking or even hearing” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a self-sufficient and adequate conclusion
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἀπόφασις denotes a determination or conclusion, not the unrelated sense “denial.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια τὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ἀνατρέψαι ἄδηλα ῥήματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: The obscure words that belong to hearing will then no longer be able to overturn the eyes’ own evidence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The obscure words are the grammatical agent, and what belongs to the eyes is the object. “Evidence” makes the substantival τὰ … ἴδια intelligible without changing the contrast between sight and hearing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will live with a guilty conscience
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb denotes living with a bad or troubled conscience, not merely living unhappily.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων σκύλλουσιν τὰς ψυχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who harass souls at the dissolution of dead bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῇ λύσει is read temporally or circumstantially, without making the harassers the explicit agents of the dissolution. “Through the dissolution of dead bodies” is a viable instrumental alternative. Reading λύσις as the release of souls from bodies is possible in context, but the supplied construction does not itself explicitly say that the necromancers release them.

passages.text: And, so that I may not recount such matters to you at great length, while I was occupied with so many reflections and circumstances, a certain report arose quietly during the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Beginning at the spring equinox, it continually grew and, truly a good messenger of God, ran throughout the world, unable to keep silent and conceal God’s will. It therefore became more widespread and greater each time, saying that a certain man in Judea, having begun at the spring equinox, was announcing to the Jews the good news of the kingdom of the everlasting God. He said that any one of them would enjoy it if he first set his way of life right. And to secure belief in him—that he did these things while full of divinity—he performed many marvelous signs and wonders by command alone, as one who had received authority from God. For he made the deaf hear and the blind see again; he made those with deformed limbs walk and set the lame upright; he drove away every disease and put every demon to flight. Even people with leprosy or scabies were healed and went away merely by fixing their gaze on him from a distance. Dead people brought to him were raised, and there was nothing he was unable to do. Indeed, the further time advanced, the far greater and more firmly established became—not the report any longer, I mean, but the truth of the matter—because of the increasing number of visitors. Assemblies were already forming in various places for deliberation and inquiry into who the one who had appeared might be and what he meant to say.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the spring equinox
lexical_decisions.rationale: τροπή can denote a seasonal turning point, including an equinox. “At the turn of spring” is a less technically specific alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος διέτρεχε τὸν κόσμον
lexical_decisions.chosen: truly a good messenger of God, ran throughout the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς ἀληθῶς is taken idiomatically as “truly” or “in truth,” affirming the report’s personification rather than introducing a comparison. ἄγγελος retains the ordinary sense “messenger”; “angel of God” is lexically possible but would make the personification more specifically supernatural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: first set his way of life right
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here concerns conduct or manner of life, while προ- supplies the prior action required before enjoying the kingdom.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ δὲ πιστεύεσθαι αὐτὸν χάριν ὅτι θειότητος γέμων ταῦτα ποιεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to secure belief in him—that he did these things while full of divinity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ὅτι clause is treated as the content to be believed. It can alternatively be read causally: “to secure belief in him, because he does these things while full of divinity.” “Full of divine power” is a possible contextual rendering of θειότης, but “divinity” preserves the source’s stronger wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he made those with deformed limbs walk and set the lame upright
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation preserves the source’s distinction between κυλλοί, people with bent or deformed limbs, and χωλοί, the lame.

lexical_decisions.chosen: people with leprosy or scabies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering reads the juxtaposed adjectives as two groups within the surrounding enumeration of afflictions: λεπροί as people with leprosy and ψωροί as people with a scabby or mangy skin condition, here rendered “scabies.” Because there is no conjunction, the words can alternatively describe one group as both leprous and scabby: “scabby leprous people.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the increasing number of visitors
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω describes people visiting or sojourning in a place. “Through more of those arriving” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Assemblies … in various places
lexical_decisions.rationale: συστήματα can denote organized groups, gatherings, or assemblies; the following deliberation and inquiry favor “assemblies.”

source_issues.issue: The printed full stop interrupts the article and its dependent genitive, where it cannot function as normal sentence punctuation. The translation provisionally treats it as intrusive editorial punctuation while preserving all the printed words.

passages.text:
And indeed, once in that very year, at the autumn equinox, someone stood up publicly and shouted, saying, “Men of Rome, listen! The Son of God is present in Judea, promising eternal life to all who desire it, if they live according to the intention of the Father who sent him. Therefore change your way—from worse things to better, from temporary things to eternal. Recognize that there is one God, the heavenly one, whose world you inhabit unjustly before his righteous eyes. But if you make this change and live according to his will, you will be carried into another age, become everlasting, and enjoy his ineffable good things. If, however, you disobey, your souls will be cast, after the dissolution of the body, into the place of fire, where, while being punished eternally, they will reorient themselves to no avail. For each person’s present life is the time for reorientation.”

As I listened to this, I was distressed that no one from among such great crowds, after hearing so momentous an announcement, had said, “I will travel to Judea so that I may see whether this man is telling the truth when he says these things.” For the claim was that the Son of God had come to Judea and, for the sake of a good and eternal hope, was revealing the will of the Father who sent him—especially since what they say he proclaims is no small matter. For he confidently affirms that the souls of some, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, while the souls of others, cast into unquenchable fire, will be punished throughout the age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in that very year
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase locates the event at or close upon the same year. “About that same year” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at the autumn equinox
lexical_decisions.rationale: As with the corresponding spring expression, τροπή denotes a seasonal turning point; “at the turn of autumn” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: change your way
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording calls for a change in manner or way of life. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω word group later in the passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν· ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: they will reorient themselves to no avail. For … the time for reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The cognate verb and noun are rendered consistently under the supplied terminology policy. “They will repent uselessly … the time for repentance” is the traditional alternative; “they will regret it to no avail” would emphasize their futile response under punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his ineffable good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόρρητος can mean secret, forbidden to disclose, or unutterable. “Ineffable” fits the transcendent benefits here while preserving their unspeakable character.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the claim was that the Son of God had come to Judea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς ὅτι can introduce reported content or give a causal explanation. The context of a public report favors reported content; “since indeed the Son of God had come” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the phrase is anarthrous here, it refers contextually to the previously identified ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ υἱός. “A son of God” remains grammatically possible if the phrase is read indefinitely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will be punished throughout the age
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the explicit noun αἰών rather than automatically assimilating it to the nearby ἀϊδίως. In this context “will be punished forever” is also semantically supportable.

source_issues.issue: The printed middle dot falls inside the article-genitive-noun phrase and interrupts “the dissolution of the body.” The translation provisionally treats it as intrusive editorial punctuation.

passages.text: While saying these things about others, I also spoke to myself: “Why do I blame others when I am under the same charge of negligence? No, I will set out for Judea after first arranging my own affairs.” Yet although I had resolved on this course, a long period of delay followed, because the affairs of life were difficult to disentangle. At last, then, I somehow reflected on the nature of life: by entangling those who are eager in hope, it lies in wait for them. Moreover, I reflected on how long I had been stealthily drawn in while being tossed about by hopes, and on the fact that we human beings die while occupied in this way. Leaving all my affairs just as they happened to be, I hurried to Portus. After reaching the harbor and putting out to sea, I was carried by the winds’ hostility to Alexandria instead of Judea. Held there for lack of winds, I spent time with the philosophers and recounted the accounts concerning both the report and the man who had appeared in Rome. They replied, “We do not know the man who appeared in Rome. But about the one who had been in Judea and whom the report calls the Son of God, we have also heard from many who have come from there as well, and we have learned about all the wonders he performed by speaking.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after first arranging my own affairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: διατίθημι with βίος can refer to putting one’s life in order. The following practical delays favor arranging personal affairs rather than an exclusively moral sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I somehow reflected on the nature of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡδίποτε is taken adverbially as “somehow or other.” The unusual expression is intelligible without conjectural alteration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by entangling those who are eager in hope, it lies in wait for them
lexical_decisions.rationale: Life remains the implied subject of both participle and verb. “Those who hurry” is the more literal alternative for τοὺς σπεύδοντας.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: how long I had been stealthily drawn in while being tossed about by hopes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative ὃν … χρόνον is read as duration and represented by “how long,” rather than as the direct object of εἰσεκλάπην. The verb is given its inward and surreptitious force as “had been stealthily drawn in.” “Had slipped in unnoticed” is possible if the passive form is understood intransitively, while “had been inveigled” is another contextual possibility; the destination or situation entered is not expressed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Portus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The capitalized Πόρτον is treated as Portus, Rome’s harbor settlement, rather than translated generically as “to the port.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the winds’ hostility
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the source’s personifying image rather than reducing the phrase to “because of adverse winds.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῆς φήμης καὶ τοῦ ἐν Ῥώμῃ φανέντος ἔλεγον τοὺς λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: recounted the accounts concerning both the report and the man who had appeared in Rome
lexical_decisions.rationale: The syntax is somewhat redundant, but λόγους can denote accounts concerning both topics. “Related what the report said and the words of the man” is possible, though it more strongly makes the second genitive possessive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ἐν Ἰουδαίᾳ γενομένου καὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης λεγομένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who had been in Judea and whom the report calls the Son of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης explicitly identifies the report as the source of the designation “Son of God.” The broader γενομένου is rendered neutrally as “had been”; “had appeared” or “had emerged” is possible in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ παρὰ πολλῶν τῶν κἀκεῖθεν ἐληλυθότων ἠκούσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we have also heard from many who have come from there as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: The additive wording is retained without supplying an unexpressed first source for ἠκούσαμεν. That first point of comparison could be Clement’s account or another source; ὑπὸ τῆς φήμης belongs explicitly to the preceding designation, not necessarily to the verb “we have heard.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wonders he performed by speaking
lexical_decisions.rationale: The circumstantial participle λαλῶν can express means, yielding miracles performed by speech. “The wonders he performed while speaking” is also grammatically possible.

source_issues.source_quote: οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε
source_issues.issue: The printed full stop separates καί from the following relative construction, leaving the latter as an abrupt fragment. The translation provisionally treats the stop as intrusive editorial punctuation while retaining the difficult wording that follows.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃν ποτε

source_issues.source_quote: ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος
source_issues.issue: The supplied wording is lexically and syntactically unusual but is retained unchanged. The translation provisionally reads χρόνον as an accusative of duration and εἰσεκλάπην with passive inward or surreptitious-entry force. An intransitive understanding such as “had slipped in unnoticed” remains possible; no conjectural correction is proposed.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
