passages.text: You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with them and rebuke them for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires, so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to consume the things that are against desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like useless servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: may be able to consume the things that are against desire.
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ substantivizes the following prepositional phrase, and κατά with the supplied genitive τῆς naturally means against. The formal grouping preserves that syntax without silently replacing the genitive with an accusative or moving opposition to qualify the consuming action. Its precise intended sense remains difficult in the surrounding fire-and-desire argument; things belonging to desire would require a textual or syntactic account not established by this wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: become angry with them and rebuke them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied αὐτοῖς is third-person them, not reflexive αὑτοῖς. The English retains the anaphoric pronoun without independently naming its antecedent. The prior self-directed rendering is not retained because the supplied spelling and context do not establish it; a reflexive reading would require separate grammatical or textual support, not silent accent alteration.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated
lexical_decisions.rationale: So that explicitly keeps the purpose or intended-result link of ἵνα with the preceding anger and rebuke, not an independent assured future result. The fire/uncultivated-field comparison remains intact.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
source_issues.issue: The formal grouping the things that are against desire is defensible from the supplied article and genitive construction, but its fit with the surrounding fire-and-desire argument is difficult. This translation does not claim to resolve that difficulty or emend the Greek. The previous adverbial attachment is not retained, because an independent object for τὰ was not adequately established.

passages.text: For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God; for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: In you explicitly preserves ὑμῖν as the recipients of the sowing, separately from the earlier location of the lurking evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια is a supposition, notion, or suspicion; supposed understanding preserves that cognitive claim rather than introducing a deliberate display or pretension. For retains the explanatory γάρ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Examine preserves the testing, scrutiny, or questioning force of ἐτάσωμεν instead of general deal with. Its dative complement is understood as the target or concern of the examination, with the lurking/sowing participles describing that evil. The English object construction makes this contextual relation readable without changing the printed dative or diagnosing an OCR defect. Question or put to the test are viable lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Be reconciled with yourselves:
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads plural ἑαυτοῖς reflexively because the surrounding argument concerns evil, ignorance, and irrational desire within the hearers. Be reconciled with one another is the material reciprocal alternative, also possible with the plural reflexive. Neither reading is presented as uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία·
lexical_decisions.chosen: Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God;
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχθρα is the noun enmity, not adjective ἐχθρά. A kind preserves the indefinite τις and the nominal classification of desire as enmity, rather than introducing only the existence of a hostile desire.

passages.text: Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully, is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you look to heaven for everything and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both printed ἢ disjunctions remain. The child relationship is inferred from the ensuing explicit son, not restored from missing text; the redundant father remains the supplied reading. Taking the first ἢ as conjectural ᾖ would create a smoother alternative, but that conjecture is not adopted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Once clear-minded keeps νήψας circumstantial. The main text reads the question as a reductio of the proposed obligation to preserve ancestral practices and attaches the second μή to ποιῶν: not repeating parental conduct would be treated as sin under that argument. The full material alternative reads οὐκ ὀφείλει as a rhetorical obligation question and the second μή as negating the clause ending in ἀμαρτάνῃ: Is the son, once clear-minded, not obliged to choose the better course, so that he does not act impiously and does not sin by doing the same things as his parents? That reading instead makes repeating the parents’ conduct the sin to avoid. Both scope decisions are disclosed; neither implies a source-corruption claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: look to heaven for everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter accusative τὰ πάντα qualifies the scope of looking, not the nominative people looking. Looking wholly toward heaven is another viable adverbial rendering; for everything is selected in the petition-for-rain context.

passages.text: No: rather, do more, so that if those in error do not murder, we do not even become angry; if the person in error does not commit adultery, we do not even think of it in the first place; if the person in error loves the one who loves him, we also love those who hate us; if the person in error lends to those who have, we also lend to those who do not have. In short, we who hope to inherit the boundless age ought to do better than the good things done by those who know only the present age. We know that if their deeds, examined alongside our deeds on the day of judgment, are found equal in good conduct, we too must be put to shame, while they, through error having done what is against them, must perish. I spoke of being put to shame in this respect: we did not do more than they did, although we also knew more than they did. But if we are to be put to shame for displaying good conduct equal to theirs and not more, how much more if we display less good conduct than theirs?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἐλπίζοντες κληρονομεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we who hope to inherit the boundless age
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπειρος means boundless or endless; αἰών remains age, contrasting the present age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we also knew more than they did
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὧν is the comparative genitive supplying the comparison for πλεῖον ἐγνώκαμεν, not an object meaning knowledge about those people. Although in the main sentence makes the contextual contrast of greater knowledge but insufficient greater deeds readable; it is not a new independent fact.

lexical_decisions.chosen: good conduct
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three inflected occurrences of εὐποιία in this passage all use good conduct, preserving the repeated criterion in the equal/more/less comparison. Doing good and good deeds are legitimate general glosses, but unexplained variation here would conceal that repetition; good conduct is selected because each occurrence evaluates the parties’ comparative practice.

passages.text: That on the day of judgment the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived, the one who does not lie himself taught us ...., saying to those who neglected to come and listen to him, “The queen of the south will rise with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here, and you do not believe.” To those among the people who were unwilling to reorient at his proclamation, he said, “Men of Nineveh will rise with this generation and condemn it, because on hearing they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation; and look, something greater ... is here, and no one believes.” Thus, setting over against each of their acts of impiety those from the nations who had acted, to condemn those in reverence toward God who had not done even as much good as those who had been deceived, he admonished those with understanding not merely to do good things equally with the nations, but to do more. My discourse flowed on, taking its starting point from the need to observe menstrual separation and to immerse oneself after intercourse: not to reject such purity even if those who have been deceived practice it, since those in error who do good serve to condemn those in reverence toward God, although they themselves are not saved. For their honoring of purity is because of error, not because of worship of the true Father and God of all.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who does not lie himself taught us ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition has four gap dots; exactly four remain, without reconstruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and look, something greater ... is here
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three gap dots remain. No familiar proper name from another witness is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology, traditionally repented, preserving the stated occasion of the response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: although they themselves are not saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit non-salvation claim about people in error who nonetheless do good.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purity context concerns observance of menstrual separation, not merely monitoring a cycle. The menstrual period is a viable temporal rendering; if the noun is taken personally, the menstruating woman is another possible referent. The main text selects the separation observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their honoring of purity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context of people practicing purity supports τιμή as their valuing or honoring the practice, with αὐτῶν related to that honoring. The esteem or value of their purity, attaching αὐτῶν to ἁγνείας, is a material alternative and is not excluded by the main rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταῖς τῶν πεπλανημένων εὐποιίαις αἱ τῶν ἀλήθειαν ἐγνωκότων ἰσάζονται πράξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: Placed on an equal footing preserves the equality force of ἰσάζονται, central to the subsequent equal-good versus doing-more argument. It does not decide that every particular action necessarily receives an identical valuation; measured against alone would state comparison without the explicit equal-footing force.

source_issues.issue: Exactly 4 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.
Exactly 3 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.

The selected edition supplies an isolated dot before τῆς. English reads the phrase with this generation across that punctuation. This single dot is distinguished from the section’s four-dot and three-dot printed gaps; it is not called an OCR error and no replacement Greek is proposed.

passages.source_text: οὐχ ἄλλως δὲ τὸ πολὺ τῆς σπουδῆς πρὸς κάθαρσιν ὑμῶν ἀναδέξασθαι ὑπομενεῖτε, ἐὰν μήγε αὐτοῖς ὀργισθέντες ἐπιπλήξητε περὶ ὧν ὡς ἀχρεῖοι δοῦλοι ἐνηδρεύθητε συνθέμενοι ταῖς κακαῖς ὑμῶν ἐπιθυμίαις, ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε. εἰ μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἔχετε δίκαιον πῦρ (τὴν κατὰ τῶν κακῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν ὀργὴν λέγω), μάθετε ἀπὸ ποίων καλῶν ἐνηδρεύθητε καὶ πρὸς ποίαν κόλασιν κατηρτίσθητε καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος ἠπατήθητε, καὶ οὕτως ὑμῶν ὁ νοῦς νήψας καὶ ὥσπερ πῦρ ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ πέμψαντος ἡμᾶς διδασκαλίας ἐξαφθεὶς εἰς ὀργήν, τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ. πιστεύσατέ μοι. ὅτι θελήσαντες πάντα κατορθῶσαι δυνήσεσθε.

κἂν γὰρ τῇ τοῦ σώματος λύσει τὴν κόλασιν ἐκφύγητε, πῶς τὴν ψυχὴν ὑμῶν ἄφθαρτον οὖσαν διὰ τῆς φθορᾶς φυγεῖν δυνήσεσθε; ἀθάνατος γὰρ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τῶν ἀσεβῶν, οἷς ἄμεινον ἦν μὴ ἄφθαρτον αὐτὴν ἔχειν. κολαζομένη γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀσβέστου πυρὸς ἀπεράντῳ τιμωρίᾳ καὶ μὴ θνήσκουσα, ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει. ἀλλ’ ἴσως ἐρεῖ τις ὑμῶν Φοβεῖς ἡμᾶς, Πέτρε. διδάξατε οὖν ἡμᾶς πῶς σιγῶντες ἐροῦμεν τὰ ὄντα ὡς ἔστιν· ἄλλως γὰρ αὐτὰ ὑμῖν σημαίνειν οὐ δυνάμεθα. ἐάν τε σιγήσωμεν, ἐνεδρεύεσθε ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶν διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν — ἐάν τε λαλήσωμεν, ὡς ἐπὶ ψευδεῖ ὑποθέσει φοβοῦντες ὑμᾶς ὑποπτευόμεθα. πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας προφάσει τῆς πρὸς θεὸν φιλίας; διαλλάγητε ἑαυτοῖς· ὑπὲρ γὰρ τῆς ὑμῶν σωτηρίας γίνεται ἡ μετὰ εὐποιΐας πρὸς αὐτὸν καταφυγή. ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία· ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.

ἄλλοι δὲ λέγουσιν Ἀσεβεῖν μέλλομεν, ἐὰν τὰ παραδοθέντα ἡμῖν ἐκ πατέρων σεβάσματα καταλείψωμεν· ὅμοιον γὰρ ἐστὶν τῷ παραθήκην φυλάξαι. οὐκοῦν τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου, οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ; πῶς δὲ ἀνόητοι οἱ λέγοντες Ταῦτα προσκυνοῦμεν, ἵνα μὴ αὐτῷ ὀχλῶμεν; ὡς ὀχλουμένου θεοῦ ἐφ’ οἷς εὐφημεῖται, μὴ ὀχλουμένου δὲ ἐφ’ οἷς ἀχαριστούμενος βλασφημεῖται. διὰ τί οὖν, ὁπόταν ἐποχὴ ὑετοῦ γένηται, πρὸς οὐρανὸν τὰ πάντα ἀφορῶντες εὐχὰς καὶ λιτὰς ἀπονέμετε; καὶ ὅταν ἐπιτύχητε, τάχιον ἐπιλανθάνεσθε; ἀμήσαντες γὰρ ἢ τρυγήσαντες εὐθέως τοῖς μηδὲν οὖσιν εἰδώλοις τὰς ἀπαρχὰς ἀπονέμετε, τάχιον ἐπιλανθανόμενοι τοῦ εὐεργετήσαντος θεοῦ. καὶ οὕτως εἰς ἄλση καὶ εἰς τοὺς ναοὺς γενόμενοι θυσίας ἐπιτελοῦντες εὐωχεῖσθε. διὰ τοῦτο οἱ μὲν ὑμῶν λέγουσιν Παρηγορίας καὶ τοῦ εὐωχεῖσθαι χάριν καλῶς ταῦτα ἐπινενοήται.

οὐχί, ἀλλὰ τὸ πλεῖον, ἵνα ἐὰν οἱ ἐν πλάνῃ μὴ φονεύωσιν, ἡμεῖς μηδὲ ὀργιζώμεθα — ἐὰν ὁ ἐν πλάνῃ μὴ μοιχεύῃ, ἡμεῖς τὴν ἀρχὴν μηδὲ ἐνθυμηθῶμεν — ἐὰν ὁ ἐν πλάνῃ τὸν ἀγαπῶντα ἀγαπᾷ, ἡμεῖς καὶ τοὺς μισοῦντας — ἐὰν ὁ ἐν πλάνῃ δανείζῃ τοῖς ἔχουσιν, ἡμεῖς καὶ τοῖς μὴ ἔχουσιν· ἁπαξαπλῶς ὀφείλομεν οἱ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἐλπίζοντες κληρονομεῖν τῶν τὸν παρόντα μόνον εἰδότων τῶν ὑπὸ αὐτῶν γενομένων καλῶν κρεῖττον ποιεῖν, εἰδότες ὅτι ἐὰν αὐτῶν τὰ ἔργα τοῖς ἡμετέροις ἔργοις ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως ἀνακριθέντα ἴσα τῇ εὐποιίᾳ εὑρεθῇ, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἐναισχυνθῆναι ἔχομεν, αὐτοὶ δὲ διὰ πλάνην τὰ καθ’ αὐτῶν ποιήσαντες ἀπολέσθαι. τὸ δὲ αἰσχυνθῆναι κατὰ τοῦτο εἴρηκα ὅτι μὴ πλεῖον ἐποιήσαμεν αὐτῶν, ὧν καὶ πλεῖον ἐγνώκαμεν. εἰ δὲ αἰσχυνθῆναι ἔστιν τὴν εὐποιίαν αὐτοῖς ἴσην δείξαντας καὶ οὐ πλεῖον, πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον, ἐὰν αὐτῶν τῆς εὐποιίας τὸ ἧττον δείξωμεν;

ὅτι δὲ ὄντως ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως ταῖς τῶν πεπλανημένων εὐποιίαις αἱ τῶν ἀλήθειαν ἐγνωκότων ἰσάζονται πράξεις, αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀψευδὴς ἐδίδαξεν...., εἰπὼν πρὸς μὲν τοὺς ἀμελοῦντας ἐλθεῖν καὶ ἐπακούειν αὐτοῦ „βασίλισσα νότου ἐγερθήσεται μετὰ .τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης καὶ κατακρινεῖ αὐτήν, ὅτι ἦλθεν ἀπὸ τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς ἀκοῦσαι τὴν σοφίαν Σολομῶνος· καὶ ἰδοὺ πλεῖον Σολομῶνος ὧδε, καὶ οὐ πιστεύετε“. πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἐν τῷ λαῷ μὴ θέλοντας μετανοῆσαι ἐπὶ τῷ κηρύγματι αὐτοῦ εἶπεν „ἄνδρες Νινευῖται ἐγερθήσονται μετὰ τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης καὶ κατακρινοῦσιν αὐτήν, ὅτι ἀκούσαντες μετενόησαν εἰς τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰωνᾶ· καὶ ἰδοὺ πλεῖον ... ὧδε, καὶ οὐδεὶς πιστεύει“. καὶ οὕτως πρὸς πᾶσαν ἀσέβειαν αὐτῶν ἀντιπαραθεὶς τοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐθνῶν πεποιηκότας εἰς κατάκρισιν τῶν ἐν θεοσεβείᾳ μηδὲ τὸ ἴσον καλὸν τοῖς πεπλανημένοις πεποιηκότων, τοὺς ἔχοντας λογισμὸν ἐνουθέτει μὴ μόνον ὅσα τοῖς ἔθνεσιν τὰ καλὰ ἴσως ποιεῖν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πλεῖον. ὁ δὲ λόγος μοι ἐρρύη, πρόφασιν λαβὼν ἐκ τοῦ δεῖν φυλάσσειν τὴν ἄφεδρον καὶ ἀπὸ κοινωνίας βαπτίζεσθαι, μὴ ἀρνεῖσθαι τὴν τοιαύτην ἁγνείαν, κἂν οἱ πεπλανημένοι αὐτὴν πράττωσιν, ὅτε εἰς κατάκρισιν τῶν ἐν θεοσεβείᾳ εἰσὶν οἱ ἐν πλάνῃ ποιοῦντες καλῶς μετὰ τοῦ μὴ σῴζεσθαι· ὅτι ἡ τιμὴ τῆς ἁγνείας αὐτῶν ἐστὶ διὰ τὴν πλάνην καὶ οὐ διὰ θρησκείαν τοῦ ὄντως πατρὸς καὶ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with them and rebuke them for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires, so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to consume the things that are against desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like useless servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: may be able to consume the things that are against desire.
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ substantivizes the following prepositional phrase, and κατά with the supplied genitive τῆς naturally means against. The formal grouping preserves that syntax without silently replacing the genitive with an accusative or moving opposition to qualify the consuming action. Its precise intended sense remains difficult in the surrounding fire-and-desire argument; things belonging to desire would require a textual or syntactic account not established by this wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: become angry with them and rebuke them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied αὐτοῖς is third-person them, not reflexive αὑτοῖς. The English retains the anaphoric pronoun without independently naming its antecedent. The prior self-directed rendering is not retained because the supplied spelling and context do not establish it; a reflexive reading would require separate grammatical or textual support, not silent accent alteration.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated
lexical_decisions.rationale: So that explicitly keeps the purpose or intended-result link of ἵνα with the preceding anger and rebuke, not an independent assured future result. The fire/uncultivated-field comparison remains intact.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
source_issues.issue: The formal grouping the things that are against desire is defensible from the supplied article and genitive construction, but its fit with the surrounding fire-and-desire argument is difficult. This translation does not claim to resolve that difficulty or emend the Greek. The previous adverbial attachment is not retained, because an independent object for τὰ was not adequately established.

passages.text: For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God; for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: In you explicitly preserves ὑμῖν as the recipients of the sowing, separately from the earlier location of the lurking evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια is a supposition, notion, or suspicion; supposed understanding preserves that cognitive claim rather than introducing a deliberate display or pretension. For retains the explanatory γάρ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Examine preserves the testing, scrutiny, or questioning force of ἐτάσωμεν instead of general deal with. Its dative complement is understood as the target or concern of the examination, with the lurking/sowing participles describing that evil. The English object construction makes this contextual relation readable without changing the printed dative or diagnosing an OCR defect. Question or put to the test are viable lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Be reconciled with yourselves:
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads plural ἑαυτοῖς reflexively because the surrounding argument concerns evil, ignorance, and irrational desire within the hearers. Be reconciled with one another is the material reciprocal alternative, also possible with the plural reflexive. Neither reading is presented as uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία·
lexical_decisions.chosen: Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God;
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχθρα is the noun enmity, not adjective ἐχθρά. A kind preserves the indefinite τις and the nominal classification of desire as enmity, rather than introducing only the existence of a hostile desire.

passages.text: Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully, is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you look to heaven for everything and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both printed ἢ disjunctions remain. The child relationship is inferred from the ensuing explicit son, not restored from missing text; the redundant father remains the supplied reading. Taking the first ἢ as conjectural ᾖ would create a smoother alternative, but that conjecture is not adopted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Once clear-minded keeps νήψας circumstantial. The main text reads the question as a reductio of the proposed obligation to preserve ancestral practices and attaches the second μή to ποιῶν: not repeating parental conduct would be treated as sin under that argument. The full material alternative reads οὐκ ὀφείλει as a rhetorical obligation question and the second μή as negating the clause ending in ἀμαρτάνῃ: Is the son, once clear-minded, not obliged to choose the better course, so that he does not act impiously and does not sin by doing the same things as his parents? That reading instead makes repeating the parents’ conduct the sin to avoid. Both scope decisions are disclosed; neither implies a source-corruption claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: look to heaven for everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter accusative τὰ πάντα qualifies the scope of looking, not the nominative people looking. Looking wholly toward heaven is another viable adverbial rendering; for everything is selected in the petition-for-rain context.

passages.text: No: rather, do more, so that if those in error do not murder, we do not even become angry; if the person in error does not commit adultery, we do not even think of it in the first place; if the person in error loves the one who loves him, we also love those who hate us; if the person in error lends to those who have, we also lend to those who do not have. In short, we who hope to inherit the boundless age ought to do better than the good things done by those who know only the present age. We know that if their deeds, examined alongside our deeds on the day of judgment, are found equal in good conduct, we too must be put to shame, while they, through error having done what is against them, must perish. I spoke of being put to shame in this respect: we did not do more than they did, although we also knew more than they did. But if we are to be put to shame for displaying good conduct equal to theirs and not more, how much more if we display less good conduct than theirs?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἐλπίζοντες κληρονομεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we who hope to inherit the boundless age
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπειρος means boundless or endless; αἰών remains age, contrasting the present age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we also knew more than they did
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὧν is the comparative genitive supplying the comparison for πλεῖον ἐγνώκαμεν, not an object meaning knowledge about those people. Although in the main sentence makes the contextual contrast of greater knowledge but insufficient greater deeds readable; it is not a new independent fact.

lexical_decisions.chosen: good conduct
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three inflected occurrences of εὐποιία in this passage all use good conduct, preserving the repeated criterion in the equal/more/less comparison. Doing good and good deeds are legitimate general glosses, but unexplained variation here would conceal that repetition; good conduct is selected because each occurrence evaluates the parties’ comparative practice.

passages.text: That on the day of judgment the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived, the one who does not lie himself taught us ...., saying to those who neglected to come and listen to him, “The queen of the south will rise with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here, and you do not believe.” To those among the people who were unwilling to reorient at his proclamation, he said, “Men of Nineveh will rise with this generation and condemn it, because on hearing they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation; and look, something greater ... is here, and no one believes.” Thus, setting over against each of their acts of impiety those from the nations who had acted, to condemn those in reverence toward God who had not done even as much good as those who had been deceived, he admonished those with understanding not merely to do good things equally with the nations, but to do more. My discourse flowed on, taking its starting point from the need to observe menstrual separation and to immerse oneself after intercourse: not to reject such purity even if those who have been deceived practice it, since those in error who do good serve to condemn those in reverence toward God, although they themselves are not saved. For their honoring of purity is because of error, not because of worship of the true Father and God of all.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who does not lie himself taught us ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition has four gap dots; exactly four remain, without reconstruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and look, something greater ... is here
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three gap dots remain. No familiar proper name from another witness is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology, traditionally repented, preserving the stated occasion of the response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: although they themselves are not saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit non-salvation claim about people in error who nonetheless do good.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purity context concerns observance of menstrual separation, not merely monitoring a cycle. The menstrual period is a viable temporal rendering; if the noun is taken personally, the menstruating woman is another possible referent. The main text selects the separation observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their honoring of purity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context of people practicing purity supports τιμή as their valuing or honoring the practice, with αὐτῶν related to that honoring. The esteem or value of their purity, attaching αὐτῶν to ἁγνείας, is a material alternative and is not excluded by the main rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταῖς τῶν πεπλανημένων εὐποιίαις αἱ τῶν ἀλήθειαν ἐγνωκότων ἰσάζονται πράξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: Placed on an equal footing preserves the equality force of ἰσάζονται, central to the subsequent equal-good versus doing-more argument. It does not decide that every particular action necessarily receives an identical valuation; measured against alone would state comparison without the explicit equal-footing force.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

passages.text: Some say, “If he did not want them to exist, they would not exist, but would have been destroyed.” I too say that this certainly will happen when everyone has displayed his own choice toward him; then the present world will be changed. Yet even if you wanted him to act in this way, so that none of the things worshiped existed, tell us: which existing thing have you not worshiped? Do not some of you worship the sun, others the moon, others water, others earth, others mountains, others plants, others seeds, and others even a human being, as in Egypt? Then God would have had to leave nothing, not even us, so that there would be neither anything worshiped nor anyone worshiping. Truly, this is what the terrible serpent lurking within you wants to happen; he does not spare you. But it will not be so. For the thing worshiped commits no sin: it suffers violence at the hands of the person who wants to worship it. Even if all human beings judge unjustly, God does not. For it is not just for the one who suffers and the one who inflicts it to receive the same punishment—unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αὐτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν δείξωσιν προαίρεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: has displayed his own choice toward him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains human choice and its orientation toward God without inserting a doctrine of predestination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀναδέξηται τὴν τοῦ μόνου τιμιωτάτου τιμήν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The exception concerns a recipient of worship willingly accepting divine honor. No named example is added.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “the worshipers themselves ought to be destroyed by the true God, so that no one else does this.” But you are not wiser than God, so as to offer him advice as someone more intelligent. He knows what he is doing. For he is patient with all who live in impiety, like a merciful father who loves humanity, knowing that even impious people become reverent. Many of the very people who revere shameful and insensible things have become clear-minded, stopped revering them and sinning, and taken refuge in the true God; through prayers and good deeds they have been saved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have become clear-minded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB clear-minded rendering for awakening from religious error, not an exclusively literal sobriety claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through prayers and good deeds they have been saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit linkage of salvation, prayers, and good deeds without imposing a denominational explanation.

passages.text: “But from the beginning he ought to have made us not even think about such things at all.” In saying this, you do not know what freedom of choice is or how it is possible to be truly good. For the person who is good by his own choice is truly good; the person made good by someone else’s compulsion is not truly so, because he is not what he is by his own choice. Since each person’s freedom produces what is truly good and reveals what is truly evil, God has arranged, through the circumstances, for becoming an enemy or a friend to lie within each person. “No,” someone says, “rather, he himself makes us think everything that we think.” Stop! What further blasphemy are you speaking when you say this? For if everything we think is put into effect in us by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy. Stop speaking ill of him, you who ought to speak well of him and assign him every honor. And do not say, “God does not claim honor.” Even if he claims nothing, we still ought, with an eye to what is just, to repay with a thankful voice the one who has benefited us in every way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freedom of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally self-determination or being in one’s own power; the paragraph explicitly contrasts personal choice and external compulsion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποθέσεις can denote situations, underlying conditions, or proposed matters; circumstances fits the arrangements in which choice operates without specifying their exact mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves distinct vice categories without embellishing sexual content or reducing all three to a generic evil.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “we do better by thanking him and everyone else together.” In saying this, you do not know the plot against you. For suppose many physicians promise to treat one sick person but can do nothing, while one who really can heal does not administer his remedy, reasoning that if he heals the patient, others will take the credit. In the same way, when God is esteemed along with many who can do nothing, he does not bestow benefits. “What then?” someone says. “Is God indignant about this, if someone else gets the credit when he heals?” I say that even if he is not indignant, he still does not wish to become an accomplice in deception. For when he does good, the idol that has done nothing is also confirmed as having power. I too say that if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this. So become clear-minded for the sake of salvation and think what is reasonable. For God, being without need, himself needs nothing and is not harmed. It is we who benefit or are harmed. Just as Caesar is neither harmed when he is reviled nor benefited when he is thanked, but safety belongs to the one who thanks him and destruction to the one who reviles him, so those who speak well of God do not benefit him at all but save themselves. Likewise, those who blaspheme do him no injury but are themselves destroyed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ φυσικῶς ἠδίκητο πρὸς ἀναίσθητα ἐπτοημένος, ἴσως ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ὑπομεμενήκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of being harmed and infatuated is understood as the worshiper, while the subject of putting up with this is God, who immediately afterward is explicitly said not to suffer harm. φυσικῶς can also mean naturally. The Greek leaves these subjects implicit, so this contextual subject differentiation is disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Caesar
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the imperial name/title without identifying a particular emperor.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “it is not the same with a human being and God.” I agree that it is not the same. For the punishment is greater for having shown irreverence toward one who is greater, and less for the one who has sinned against someone lesser. Thus, just as God is greater than all, the person who has shown irreverence toward him will undergo greater punishment for having sinned against someone greater. It is not that God retaliates with his own hand; rather, all creation is indignant at this and pursues the offender by its nature. For neither will the sun give the blasphemer light, nor the earth its fruits, nor a spring its water, nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest, since even now, while the world’s allotted term still stands, all creation shares in the indignation. Therefore neither does heaven provide rain in full nor the earth its fruits, and most people are consequently brought to ruin. Even the air itself, inflamed with anger, changes to act as a pestilence. Yet whatever good things we enjoy, he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us. This is how all creation is angry with you who dishonor the maker of all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν ᾅδῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ ἐκεῖ καθεστὼς ἄρχων τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Hades as the source’s named realm; it is not replaced by a later, more specific doctrine of hell.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου προθεσμίας ὑφεστώσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: while the world’s allotted term still stands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated time-limit belongs to the world; the text does not supply its length.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτοῦ ἐλέῳ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν φιλανθρωπίαν βιάζεται τὴν κτίσιν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive/possessive references are retained contextually: God compels creation toward humane treatment of us. The active force of βιάζεται is not softened into permission.

findings.source_quote: εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα, αὐτὸν αἴτιον λέγετε πορνειῶν, ἀσελγειῶν, πλεονεξιῶν καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας.
findings.english_quote: For if everything we think is put into effect in us by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy.
findings.issue: The subject of ἐνεργούμεθα is “we”: the conditional concerns our being moved or actuated by God in everything we think. The draft instead makes our thoughts the things “put into effect,” introducing their implementation rather than faithfully stating the source’s claim about divine agency in our thinking.
findings.suggested_revision: Replace the sentence with: “For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy.” This proposed wording requires fresh review.

passages.source_text: τινὲς δὲ λέγουσιν Εἰ μὴ ἤθελεν αὐτὰ εἶναι, οὐκ ἂν ἦν, ἀλλ’ ἀνῃρεῖτο ἄν. φημὶ κἀγώ· τοῦτο πάντως ἔσται, ὅταν πάντες τὴν αὐτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν δείξωσιν προαίρεσιν, καὶ οὕτως ἀλλαγὴ τοῦ νῦν γενήσεται κόσμου. πλὴν εἰ καὶ οὕτως ἠθέλετε αὐτὸν ποιῆσαι, ἵνα μηδὲν τῶν προσκυνουμένων ὑπῆρχεν: εἴπατε ἡμῖν τί τῶν ὄντων οὐκ ἐθρησκεύσατε; οὐχ οἱ μὲν ὑμῶν τὸν ἥλιον, οἱ δὲ σελήνην, οἱ δὲ ὕδωρ, οἱ δὲ γῆν, οἱ δὲ τὰ ὄρη, οἱ δὲ φυτά, οἱ δὲ τὰ σπέρματα, οἱ δὲ καὶ ἄνθρωπον (ὡς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ) προσκυνοῦσιν; ἐχρῆν οὖν τὸν θεὸν μηδὲν ἐᾶσαι, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ ἡμᾶς, ἵνα μηδὲν ἂν ἦν τὸ προσκυνούμενον μήτε τὸ προσκυνοῦν. ἀληθῶς τοῦτο βούλεται γενέσθαι ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν δεινὸς ἐνδομυχῶν ὄφις, ὃς οὐ φείδεται ὑμῶν. ἀλλ’ οὐχ οὕτως ἔσται. οὐδὲν γὰρ ἁμαρτάνει τὸ προσκυνούμενον· βίαν γὰρ πάσχει ὑπὸ τοῦ προσκυνεῖν αὐτὸ θέλοντος. εἰ γὰρ ὑπὸ πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἄδικος γίνεται κρίσις, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὑπὸ θεοῦ. οὐ γὰρ δίκαιόν ἐστιν τὴν αὐτὴν τιμωρίαν ἀναδέξασθαι τὸν πάσχοντα καὶ τὸν διαθέμενον, ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀναδέξηται τὴν τοῦ μόνου τιμιωτάτου τιμήν.

ἀλλὰ (φησίν) ἐχρῆν αὐτοὺς τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας ἀναιρεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ ὄντως θεοῦ, ἵνα ἄλλος τοῦτο μὴ ποιῇ. ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἶ σοφώτερος τοῦ θεοῦ, ἵνα αὐτῷ ὡς φρονιμώτερος γνώμην δῷς. οἶδεν ὃ ποιεῖ. πᾶσι γὰρ ἐν ἀσεβείᾳ οὖσι μακροθυμεῖ, ὡς ἐλεήμων καὶ φιλάνθρωπος πατήρ, εἰδὼς ὅτι καὶ ἐξ ἀσεβῶν εὐσεβεῖς γίνονται. καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν σεβόντων τὰ αἰσχρὰ καὶ ἀναίσθητα πολλοὶ νήψαντες τοῦ μὲν αὐτὰ σέβειν καὶ ἁμαρτάνειν ἐπαύσαντο, τῷ δὲ ὄντως θεῷ προσφυγόντες εὐχαῖς καὶ καλοῖς ἔργοις ἐσώθησαν.

ἀλλὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἔδει ποιῆσαι ἡμᾶς μηδὲ ὅλως περὶ τοιούτων ἐνθυμεῖσθαι. ταῦτα λέγοντες ἀγνοεῖτε τί ἐστιν τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, καὶ πῶς δυνατὸν ἐστιν ἀγαθοὺς τῷ ὄντι εἶναι. ὅτι ὁ ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει ὢν ἀγαθὸς ὄντως ἀγαθός ἐστιν, ὁ δὲ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου ἀνάγκης ἀγαθὸς γενόμενος ὄντως οὐκ ἔστιν, ὅτι μὴ ἰδίᾳ προαιρέσει ἐστὶν ὅ ἐστιν. ἐπεὶ οὖν τὸ ἑκάστου ἐλεύθερον ἀποτελεῖ τὸ ὄντως ἀγαθὸν καὶ δεικνύει τὸ ὄντως κακόν, ἐν ἑκάστῳ γενέσθαι ἐχθρὸν ἢ φίλον διὰ τῶν ὑποθέσεων ὁ θεὸς ἐμηχανήσατο. οὒ φησιν, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ὃ ἐνθυμούμεθα, αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς ποιεῖ νοεῖν. παύσασθε· τί πλεῖον βλασφημεῖτε οἱ τοῦτο λέγοντες; εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα, αὐτὸν αἴτιον λέγετε πορνειῶν, ἀσελγειῶν, πλεονεξιῶν καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας. παύσασθε δυσφημοῦντες, οἱ εὐφημεῖν καὶ πᾶσαν τιμὴν αὐτῷ ἀπονέμειν ὀφείλοντες. καὶ μὴ λέγετε Οὐκ ἐπιδικάζεται ὁ θεὸς τιμῆς. εἰ γὰρ αὐτὸς οὐδενὸς ἐπιδικάζεται, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε ἡμᾶς ἐχρῆν εἰς τὸ δίκαιον ἀφορῶντας τὸν ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμᾶς εὐεργετήσαντα εὐχαρίστῳ ἀμείψασθαι φωνῇ.

ἀλλὰ (φησίν) κρεῖττον ποιοῦμεν ἅμα αὐτῷ καὶ πᾶσιν εὐχαριστοῦντες. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα λέγοντες οὐκ ἴστε τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν ἐπιβουλήν. ὡς γάρ, ὁπόταν ἕνα κάμνοντα πολλοὶ ἰατροὶ θεραπεύειν ἐπαγγέλλωνται μηδὲν δυνάμενοι, εἷς δέ τις ὄντως ἰᾶσθαι δυνάμενος τὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντίδοτον μὴ προσφέρῃ, λογισάμενος ὅτι, ἂν αὐτὸς θεραπεύσῃ, ἄλλοι ἐπιγράφονται: οὕτω καὶ ὁ θεὸς μετὰ πολλῶν ἀξιούμενος τῶν μηδὲν δυναμένων οὐκ εὐεργετεῖ. τί οὖν; (φησίν) ὁ θεὸς ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἀγανακτεῖ, ἐάν γε αὐτοῦ θεραπεύοντος ἄλλος ἐπιγραφῇ; φημί, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἀγανακτεῖ, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε οὐ θέλει τῆς ἀπάτης συνεργὸς γενέσθαι. αὐτοῦ γὰρ εὐεργετήσαντος καὶ τὸ μηδὲν ποιῆσαν εἴδωλον ὡς δυνηθὲν πιστοῦται. ἀλλὰ κἀγὼ φημι ὅτι, εἰ μὴ φυσικῶς ἠδίκητο πρὸς ἀναίσθητα ἐπτοημένος, ἴσως ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ὑπομεμενήκει· διὸ νήψατε ὑπὲρ τῆς σωτηρίας τὰ εὔλογα νοεῖν. ὁ θεὸς γὰρ ἀνενδεὴς ὢν αὐτὸς οὐδενὸς δεῖται οὔτε βλάπτεται. ἡμῶν γὰρ ἐστὶν τὸ ὠφελεῖσθαι ἢ βλάπτεσθαι. ὅνπερ γὰρ τρόπον Καῖσαρ οὔτε βλασφημούμενος βλάπτεται οὔτε εὐχαριστούμενος ὠφελεῖται, ἀλλὰ τοῦ εὐχαριστοῦντος μὲν γίνεται τὸ ἀκίνδυνον, τοῦ δὲ βλασφημοῦντος ὄλεθρος: οὕτως οἱ θεὸν εὐφημοῦντες αὐτὸν μὲν οὐδὲν ὠφελοῦσιν, ἑαυτοὺς δὲ σώζουσιν, ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ βλασφημοῦντες αὐτὸν μὲν οὐκ ἀδικοῦσιν, αὐτοὶ δὲ ὀλοθρεύονται.

ἀλλὰ (φησίν) οὐχ ὁμοίως ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπου καὶ θεοῦ. σύμφημι κἀγὼ ὅτι οὐχ ὁμοίως. μείζων γὰρ ἡ κόλασις ὡς μείζονα ἀσεβήσαντι, ἥττων δὲ τῷ εἰς τὸν ἥττονα ἁμαρτήσαντι. ὡς οὖν πάντων μείζων ὁ θεός, οὕτως μείζονα ὑφέξει κόλασιν ὁ εἰς αὐτὸν ἀσεβήσας ὡς εἰς μείζονα ἁμαρτήσας, οὐκ αὐτοῦ αὐτόχειρος ἀμυνομένου, ἀλλὰ πάσης τῆς κτίσεως ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἀγανακτούσης καὶ φυσικῶς ἐπεξερχομένης. οὐ γὰρ δώσει τῷ βλασφήμῳ οὐχ ἥλιος τὸ φῶς, οὐ γῆ τοὺς καρπούς, οὐ πηγὴ τὸ ὕδωρ, οὐκ ἐν ᾅδῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ ἐκεῖ καθεστὼς ἄρχων τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν, ὁπότε καὶ νῦν ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου προθεσμίας ὑφεστώσης παραγανακτεῖ πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις. διὸ οὔτε τελείως οὐρανὸς ὑετοὺς παρέχει οὔτε γῆ τοὺς καρπούς, διὸ οἱ πλείονες λυμαίνονται. ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ ἀὴρ θυμῷ ὑπεκκαιόμενος πρὸς λοιμώδη πρᾶξιν μεταβάλλεται. πλὴν ὅσων ἀπολαύομεν ἀγαθῶν, τῷ αὐτοῦ ἐλέῳ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν φιλανθρωπίαν βιάζεται τὴν κτίσιν. οὕτως ὑμῖν τοῖς ἀτιμάζουσιν τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν ἡ πᾶσα κτίσις χαλεπαίνει.
