passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that extremely dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salt and table
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων, “of those who have revered God,” to the incomplete subject marked by ὁ ... ων. This is supported by the contrast between the appearing man and the group benefiting from immortal, painless life, but it does not restore that subject’s missing letters. A material alternative attaches the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “when he appears in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God, the [ὁ ... ων] will be able to live immortally and without pain.” Neither attachment is uniquely established; the three-dot gap remains unchanged and no lost wording is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on that extremely dreadful night
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative χαλεπωτάτῃ can be elative, “extremely dreadful,” as in 13.6. This preserves its intensity without requiring that this was the uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after I have baptized her today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative singular participle agrees with Peter, the speaker. The English explicitly makes him the baptizer, not the children. Its event is within the rhetorical question’s contemplated action, not a statement that baptism has already occurred.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως αὐτήν τε καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον αὐτῆς μεταπεμψάμενος ἐξαυτῆς βαπτίσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text construes the summoning participle as directed to the hostess and the finite baptism verb as directed to both women, because the mother is already before Peter pleading. The coordinated accusatives can more broadly be objects of both verbs: “that he summon her and her hostess and baptize them immediately.” This material alternative is preserved; the narrower participial attachment is contextual rather than uniquely expressed by the Greek, and the source is not changed.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, interrupting the continuous grammatical connection with ἀπέλαβον τέκνα. The English reads the surviving words continuously as “from the time I have recovered my own children.” The supplied Greek and its printed punctuation are not changed; no missing wording is restored. This is a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not an assertion of OCR error or publication-blocking source corruption.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will fill the husband’s place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῖς κρείττοσιν as neuter, referring to better circumstances, supported by the recovery of the children after danger and separation. “Among better things” is a more literal neuter rendering but can obscure the situational sense. The same form permits a masculine interpretation, “among better people,” which would locate them with a better group, for example their present associates, rather than characterize their circumstances. Neither interpretation is uniquely established; the legitimate-origin wording is retained separately and no particular group is named.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤπερ ἄκουσα μετὰ χρόνον ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις αὐταῖς ἀπωλλύου
lexical_decisions.chosen: than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἐπί with the dative causally: the sins cause the perishing. The surrounding contrast among chastity, sin, death, and salvation supports that reading. A circumstantial attachment is also possible, “than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins,” describing the condition in which she perishes rather than explicitly naming its cause. Neither attachment is uniquely required by the preposition alone.

passages.source_text: Σίμωνι δὲ τινὶ μάγῳ σχεδὸν σύντροφοι γενόμενοι, φιλίας ὁδῷ ἀπατηθῆναι ἐκινδυνεύσαμεν. ἔστιν δὲ τὶς περὶ ἀνθρώπου τινὸς λόγος, οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει· ὅμως ταῦτα μέν σοι, μῆτερ, ἐπὶ καιροῦ ἀκριβέστερον ἐκτεθήσεται. πλὴν μέλλουσιν ἡμῖν ἀπατᾶσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Σίμωνος ἑταῖρός τις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Πέτρου, Ζακχαῖος λεγόμενος, προσηκάμενος ἐνουθέτησεν μὴ ἀπατηθῆναι τῷ μάγῳ, ἐπελθόντι δὲ τῷ Πέτρῳ προσήγαγεν, ὅπως ἡμᾶς πληροφορήσας πείσῃ περὶ τῶν τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ διαφερόντων. διὸ καὶ σέ, μῆτερ, εὐχόμεθα ἵνα ὧν ἡμεῖς κατηξιώθημεν ἀγαθῶν, τούτων καὶ σὺ μεταλάβῃς, ὅπως κοινῇ ἁλῶν καὶ τραπέζης μεταλαβεῖν δυνηθῶμεν. αὕτη οὖν ἐστὶν ἡ αἰτία, τεκοῦσα, δι’ ἣν ἐνόμιζες ἡμᾶς τεθνάναι, τῷ ἐκείνῃ τῇ χαλεπωτάτῃ νυκτὶ ὑπὸ πειρατῶν ἀρθῆναι ἐν πελάγει, σὲ δὲ νομίζειν ἡμᾶς ἀπολωλέναι.

ταῦτα τοῦ Φαυστίνου εἰπόντος ἡ μήτηρ ἡμῶν προσέπεσεν τῷ Πέτρῳ, δεομένη καὶ ἀξιοῦσα ὅπως αὐτήν τε καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον αὐτῆς μεταπεμψάμενος ἐξαυτῆς βαπτίσῃ, ἵνα (φησίν) μηδεμία τις ἡμέρα ἄμοιρος γένηται, ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα, ἐν ᾗ μὴ συνεστιάσθην αὐτοῖς. ταῦτα οὖν καὶ ἡμῶν τῇ μητρὶ συνπαρακαλεσάντων, ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί νομίζετε; ἐγὼ μόνος ἄσπλαγχνός εἰμι ὅτι μὴ βούλομαι ὑμᾶς συνεστιασθῆναι τῇ μητρί, βαπτίσας αὐτὴν σήμερον; ἀλλὰ κἂν μίαν ἡμέραν πρὸ τοῦ βαπτισθῆναι νηστεῦσαι αὐτὴν δεῖ. καὶ ταῦτα ἐπεὶ ἁπλῶς τινὰ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς ἐφθέγξατο λόγον, ὃν ἐγὼ τῆς πίστεως αὐτῆς ἱκανὸν ἑρμηνέα συνεῖδον· ἐπεὶ πολλῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτὴν ἀφελληνισθῆναι δεῖ.

ταῦτα λέγων ὁ Πέτρος, τὴν ἀγαθὴν καὶ σώφρονα Ματτιδίαν ὑπὸ χαρᾶς δακρύουσαν ἰδών, ὡς ἐπὶ ὑπομνήσει τῶν γεγονότων λυπηθῆναι νομίσας ἔφη Θάρσει, γύναι· πολλῶν πολλὰ κακὰ παθόντων διὰ μοιχείαν οὐ διὰ σωφροσύνην πέπονθας, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐτελεύτησας. εἰ δὲ καὶ τεθνήκεις, σεσωσμένην ἂν εἶχες τὴν ψυχήν. πατρίδα Ῥώμην ἔλειπες διὰ σωφροσύνην; ἀλλὰ τῇ ταύτης προφάσει ἀλήθειαν εὗρες, τὸ διάδημα τῆς ἀϊδίου βασιλείας. ἐν βυθῷ κεκινδύνευκας; καὶ οὐκ ἐτελεύτησας, καὶ εἰ τετελευτήκεις, αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο πρὸς ψυχῆς σωτηρίαν. τέκνων ἀπελείφθης; πρὸς ὀλίγον, ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται. λιμώττουσα τροφὰς προσῄτησας; ἀλλὰ πορνείᾳ σῶμα σὸν οὐκ ἐμίανας. σῶμα σὸν ἐβασάνισας; ἀλλὰ τὴν ψυχὴν ἔσωσας. μοιχὸν ἔφυγες, ἵνα μὴ κοίτην ἀνδρὸς μιάνῃς; ἀλλὰ διὰ τὴν σωφροσύνην ὁ τὴν φυγὴν εἰδὼς θεὸς τὸν ἀνδρὸς ἀποπληρώσει τόπον. λυπηθεῖσα καὶ μονωθεῖσα πρὸς ὀλίγον ἀνδρὸς καὶ τέκνων ἀπελείφθης; ἀλλὰ τούτους πάντας ἀπολιπεῖν εἶχες προθεσμίᾳ θανάτου, κρεῖττον δὲ ὅτι διὰ σωφροσύνην ἑκοῦσα ἀπελείφθης ἤπερ ἄκουσα μετὰ χρόνον ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις αὐταῖς ἀπωλλύου.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that extremely dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salt and table
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων, “of those who have revered God,” to the incomplete subject marked by ὁ ... ων. This is supported by the contrast between the appearing man and the group benefiting from immortal, painless life, but it does not restore that subject’s missing letters. A material alternative attaches the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “when he appears in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God, the [ὁ ... ων] will be able to live immortally and without pain.” Neither attachment is uniquely established; the three-dot gap remains unchanged and no lost wording is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on that extremely dreadful night
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative χαλεπωτάτῃ can be elative, “extremely dreadful,” as in 13.6. This preserves its intensity without requiring that this was the uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after I have baptized her today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative singular participle agrees with Peter, the speaker. The English explicitly makes him the baptizer, not the children. Its event is within the rhetorical question’s contemplated action, not a statement that baptism has already occurred.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως αὐτήν τε καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον αὐτῆς μεταπεμψάμενος ἐξαυτῆς βαπτίσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text construes the summoning participle as directed to the hostess and the finite baptism verb as directed to both women, because the mother is already before Peter pleading. The coordinated accusatives can more broadly be objects of both verbs: “that he summon her and her hostess and baptize them immediately.” This material alternative is preserved; the narrower participial attachment is contextual rather than uniquely expressed by the Greek, and the source is not changed.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, interrupting the continuous grammatical connection with ἀπέλαβον τέκνα. The English reads the surviving words continuously as “from the time I have recovered my own children.” The supplied Greek and its printed punctuation are not changed; no missing wording is restored. This is a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not an assertion of OCR error or publication-blocking source corruption.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will fill the husband’s place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῖς κρείττοσιν as neuter, referring to better circumstances, supported by the recovery of the children after danger and separation. “Among better things” is a more literal neuter rendering but can obscure the situational sense. The same form permits a masculine interpretation, “among better people,” which would locate them with a better group, for example their present associates, rather than characterize their circumstances. Neither interpretation is uniquely established; the legitimate-origin wording is retained separately and no particular group is named.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤπερ ἄκουσα μετὰ χρόνον ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις αὐταῖς ἀπωλλύου
lexical_decisions.chosen: than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἐπί with the dative causally: the sins cause the perishing. The surrounding contrast among chastity, sin, death, and salvation supports that reading. A circumstantial attachment is also possible, “than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins,” describing the condition in which she perishes rather than explicitly naming its cause. Neither attachment is uniquely required by the preposition alone.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

passages.text: Nicetas, henceforth Faustinus, began to speak: “That very night, when the ship was breaking apart, as you know, some men who were not afraid to plunder in the depths picked us up and put us in a boat. Rowing, they took us sometimes along the shore and sometimes sent for provisions, bringing us to Strato’s Caesarea. There, by hunger, fear, and blows, though we were weeping, they managed to sell us, after also changing our names so that we would not rashly say anything they did not want said. A very distinguished woman named Justa, a convert to the Jews, bought us, kept us in the place of children, and diligently educated us in every branch of Greek learning. As we grew up and became sensible, we loved the religion and applied ourselves to learning, so that in discussions with the other nations we could expose their error. We also mastered the philosophers’ teachings, especially the most godless—I mean those of Epicurus and Pyrrho—so that we could refute them more effectively.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: kept us in the place of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their purchase and subsequent treatment are both retained. The text does not explicitly describe a legal adoption or manumission.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the most godless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative belongs to the narrator’s evaluation of the philosophers, not an added evaluation by the translator.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salt and table
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother by baptizing her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

passages.text: I said, “Tell us what statement she uttered that revealed her faith.” Peter said, “Her request that the hostess who had been her benefactor be baptized with her. She would not have asked for this to be given to the woman she loved unless she herself had first come to regard the gift of baptism as something great. Therefore I condemn many people when, after being baptized and saying that they believe, they do nothing worthy of faith and do not urge even those they love—I mean their wives, sons, or friends—to this. For if they have believed that God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds, they would without delay have urged those they loved to be baptized. But one of you will say, ‘They love them and care for them.’ This is foolish. Why, then, when they see them ill, being led away to death, or suffering other terrible things, do they lament and pity them? In the same way, if they had believed that eternal fire awaits those who do not worship God, they would not have stopped admonishing them, or, when they saw them disobedient, grieving over them as unbelievers, being fully assured of the punishment against them. Now, then, I will send for the hostess and question her whether she chooses to love the law conveyed through us, and then we will do what is required accordingly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζωὴν αἰώνιον σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς δωρεῖσθαι τὸν θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ βαπτίσματι
lexical_decisions.chosen: God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς is preserved alongside baptism; it can qualify the granting as connected with good works or characterize the life/gift together with them. The text’s combination is not recast as baptism only symbolizing or independently causing salvation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: This is foolish
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὔηθες can mean simple or naive as well as foolish; here it challenges the adequacy of an objection, not their loved ones’ intelligence.

passages.text: “Since your mother approaches baptism with faith, let her fast at least one day before baptism.” But she swore, “For two of the days that have passed, while telling the woman about the recognition, I was unable to partake of food because of my great joy, except for a little water yesterday alone.” Peter’s wife testified to her oath, saying, “She has indeed tasted nothing.” Aquila—or rather, henceforth Faustinianus—said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” Peter laughed and answered, “But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Perhaps, then, God, wishing our mother not to be separated from the table for even one day after recognizing us, arranged the fast beforehand. For just as she remained chaste in ignorance, doing what accords with the truth, so perhaps God has now arranged for her to fast a day beforehand, in ignorance, for the sake of the true baptism, so that from the very first day of recognizing us she may partake of salt with us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it did not take place for that purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: The loose ἤ-clause is read as giving the qualification that the earlier abstention was not for baptism. “Unless it took place for that purpose” is an alternative way of expressing the criterion, but the main text links it to the actual earlier non-baptismal fast.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a day beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine day is understood from the surrounding fasting discussion; no longer duration is added.

findings.source_quote: κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν.
findings.english_quote: There, by hunger, fear, and blows, though we were weeping, they managed to sell us, after also changing our names so that we would not rashly say anything they did not want said.
findings.issue: The draft changes the attachments within the coercion sequence. λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς explains the children's weeping, but the English makes hunger, fear, and blows the means by which the men managed the sale. It also relocates the purpose of preventing unwanted speech to the name change, whereas the Greek places that purpose with the preceding coercive treatment and then introduces the additional renaming.
findings.suggested_revision: Recast the sequence, for example: “There, with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us.” Review the revised attachments afresh.

findings.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
findings.english_quote: There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain.
findings.issue: The main text defensibly attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων to the incomplete subject represented by ὁ ... ων. However, the notes discuss the sense of βασιλείᾳ without disclosing the material alternative attachment of the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God.” The three-dot gap and surviving fragments are faithfully represented; the gap itself is not a coverage failure or a reason to require restoration.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note identifying both possible attachments of τῶν θεοσεβησάντων and explaining why the main text associates it with the incomplete subject. Distinguish that syntactic choice from recovery of missing wording. Retain the exact three-dot gap and the existing disclosure that no restoration has been supplied.

findings.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
findings.english_quote: from the time I have recovered my own children
findings.issue: The English gives a defensible continuous construction, but silently passes over the supplied edition's full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, which interrupts that construction. This is an image-checked printed punctuation feature, not evidence of an OCR error or missing wording.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source_issues note quoting “ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα”. Explain that the English reads the surviving words continuously despite the printed stop, without changing the supplied Greek or restoring any text. Classify this as a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not a publication-blocking source corruption.

findings.source_quote: ἐγὼ μόνος ἄσπλαγχνός εἰμι ὅτι μὴ βούλομαι ὑμᾶς συνεστιασθῆναι τῇ μητρί, βαπτίσας αὐτὴν σήμερον;
findings.english_quote: Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother by baptizing her today?
findings.issue: The placement of “by baptizing her today” leaves its agent unclear and readily attaches it to “you”. The Greek nominative singular βαπτίσας refers to Peter, not to the children. This ambiguity is introduced by the English rather than inherited from the Greek.
findings.suggested_revision: Make Peter the explicit baptizer, for example: “Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today?” Submit the revised sentence for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστιν τοῦτο νηστεία βαπτίσματος, ἢ μὴ δι’ αὐτὸ γέγονεν.
findings.english_quote: But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.
findings.issue: An explanatory connection between the clauses is contextually defensible, so “since” need not be rejected merely because the construction is unusual. Nevertheless, the note does not preserve an English alternative retaining the printed disjunctive ἤ. Its “unless it took place for that purpose” expresses a conditional criterion but is not transparently a rendering of the supplied ἢ μὴ clause. The distinction between direct rendering and contextual paraphrase needs disclosure; print verification is not the missing evidence.
findings.suggested_revision: Explicitly compare the causal main text with a source-transparent explanatory disjunction such as “But this is not a baptismal fast—or, rather, it did not take place for that purpose.” If “since” is retained, explain why the printed “or” is construed explanatorily and preserve the disjunctive alternative in the note. Label the “unless” formulation as a contextual paraphrase rather than an alternative supplied Greek reading. Any revised main text requires fresh review.

passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Νικήτης (ὁ τοῦ λοιποῦ Φαυστῖνος) ἤρξατο λέγειν Τῆς αὐτῆς ἐκείνης νυκτός, τοῦ πλοίου (ὡς οἶσθα) διαλυομένου, ἡμᾶς ἄνδρες τινὲς ἐν τῷ βυθῷ λῃστεύειν μὴ φοβούμενοι ἀνείλαντο καὶ ἐν σκάφῃ θέντες καὶ κώπαις ἐλαύνοντες ὁτὲ μὲν παρὰ γῆν ἔφερον, ὁτὲ δὲ καὶ τροφὰς μεταπεμπόμενοι εἰς τὴν Στράτωνος ἦγον Καισάρειαν κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν. γυνὴ δὲ τις Ἰουδαίοις προσήλυτος, ἀξιόλογος πάνυ, ὀνόματι Ἰοῦστα, ὠνησαμένη ἡμᾶς εἰς τέκνων ἐφύλαττεν τόπον καὶ πάσῃ ἑλληνικῇ παιδείᾳ μετὰ σπουδῆς ἐξεπαίδευσεν. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐφ’ ἡλικίας ἔμφρονες γενόμενοι καὶ τὴν θρησκείαν ἠγαπήσαμεν καὶ τὰ τῆς παιδείας ἐφιλοπονέσαμεν, ὅπως πρὸς τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη διαλεγόμενοι ἐλέγχειν αὐτὰ περὶ πλάνης δυνώμεθα. ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ φιλοσόφων ἠκριβώσαμεν, ἐξαιρέτως δὲ τὰ ἀθεώτατα, λέγω δὲ τὰ Ἐπικούρου καὶ Πύρρωνος, ἵνα μᾶλλον ἀνασκευάζειν δυνώμεθα.

Σίμωνι δὲ τινὶ μάγῳ σχεδὸν σύντροφοι γενόμενοι, φιλίας ὁδῷ ἀπατηθῆναι ἐκινδυνεύσαμεν. ἔστιν δὲ τὶς περὶ ἀνθρώπου τινὸς λόγος, οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει· ὅμως ταῦτα μέν σοι, μῆτερ, ἐπὶ καιροῦ ἀκριβέστερον ἐκτεθήσεται. πλὴν μέλλουσιν ἡμῖν ἀπατᾶσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ Σίμωνος ἑταῖρός τις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Πέτρου, Ζακχαῖος λεγόμενος, προσηκάμενος ἐνουθέτησεν μὴ ἀπατηθῆναι τῷ μάγῳ, ἐπελθόντι δὲ τῷ Πέτρῳ προσήγαγεν, ὅπως ἡμᾶς πληροφορήσας πείσῃ περὶ τῶν τῇ θεοσεβείᾳ διαφερόντων. διὸ καὶ σέ, μῆτερ, εὐχόμεθα ἵνα ὧν ἡμεῖς κατηξιώθημεν ἀγαθῶν, τούτων καὶ σὺ μεταλάβῃς, ὅπως κοινῇ ἁλῶν καὶ τραπέζης μεταλαβεῖν δυνηθῶμεν. αὕτη οὖν ἐστὶν ἡ αἰτία, τεκοῦσα, δι’ ἣν ἐνόμιζες ἡμᾶς τεθνάναι, τῷ ἐκείνῃ τῇ χαλεπωτάτῃ νυκτὶ ὑπὸ πειρατῶν ἀρθῆναι ἐν πελάγει, σὲ δὲ νομίζειν ἡμᾶς ἀπολωλέναι.

ταῦτα τοῦ Φαυστίνου εἰπόντος ἡ μήτηρ ἡμῶν προσέπεσεν τῷ Πέτρῳ, δεομένη καὶ ἀξιοῦσα ὅπως αὐτήν τε καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον αὐτῆς μεταπεμψάμενος ἐξαυτῆς βαπτίσῃ, ἵνα (φησίν) μηδεμία τις ἡμέρα ἄμοιρος γένηται, ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα, ἐν ᾗ μὴ συνεστιάσθην αὐτοῖς. ταῦτα οὖν καὶ ἡμῶν τῇ μητρὶ συνπαρακαλεσάντων, ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί νομίζετε; ἐγὼ μόνος ἄσπλαγχνός εἰμι ὅτι μὴ βούλομαι ὑμᾶς συνεστιασθῆναι τῇ μητρί, βαπτίσας αὐτὴν σήμερον; ἀλλὰ κἂν μίαν ἡμέραν πρὸ τοῦ βαπτισθῆναι νηστεῦσαι αὐτὴν δεῖ. καὶ ταῦτα ἐπεὶ ἁπλῶς τινὰ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς ἐφθέγξατο λόγον, ὃν ἐγὼ τῆς πίστεως αὐτῆς ἱκανὸν ἑρμηνέα συνεῖδον· ἐπεὶ πολλῶν ἡμερῶν αὐτὴν ἀφελληνισθῆναι δεῖ.

κἀγὼ ἔφην Εἰπὲ ἡμῖν τίνα ἐφθέγξατο λόγον, ὃς τὴν πίστιν αὐτῆς ἐξέφανεν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἡ ἀξίωσις αὐτῆς τοῦ συνβαπτισθῆναι αὐτῇ τὴν ξενοδόχον εὐεργέτιν. οὐκ ἂν δὲ τοῦτο τῇ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ποθουμένῃ δοθῆναι παρεκάλει, εἰ μὴ πρότερον αὐτὴ διετέθη ὡς ἐπὶ μεγάλῃ τῇ τοῦ βαπτίσματος δωρεᾷ. ὅθεν ἐγὼ πολλῶν καταγινώσκω, ὁπόταν βαπτισθέντες καὶ πιστεύειν λέγοντες μηδὲν ἄξιον πίστεως ποιῶσιν μηδὲ οὓς ἀγαπῶσιν (λέγω δὴ γυναῖκας αὐτῶν ἢ υἱοὺς ἢ φίλους) πρὸς τοῦτο προτρέπωνται. εἰ γὰρ πεπιστεύκασιν ζωὴν αἰώνιον σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς δωρεῖσθαι τὸν θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ βαπτίσματι ἀνυπερθέτως οὓς ἠγάπων προετρέποντο βαπτισθῆναι. ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις ὑμῶν Ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτοὺς καὶ φροντίζουσιν αὐτῶν. τοῦτο εὔηθές ἐστιν. ἐπεὶ τί δήποτε νοσοῦντας ὁρῶντες ἢ ἀπαγομένους τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ ἢ ἄλλα τινὰ χαλεπὰ πάσχοντας ὀδύρονται καὶ ἐλεῶσιν; οὕτως εἰ πεπιστεύκεισαν αἰώνιον πῦρ μένειν τοὺς τὸν θεὸν μὴ σέβοντας, οὐκ ἂν ἐπαύσαντο νουθετοῦντες ἢ καὶ ἀπειθοῦντας ὁρῶντες ὡς περὶ ἀπίστων ὀδυνώμενοι, τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν κόλασιν πεπληροφορημένοι. καὶ τὰ νῦν τὴν ξενοδόχον πέμψας ἀνακρινῶ, εἰ τὸν νόμον τὸν δι’ ἡμῶν ἀγαπᾶν αἱρεῖται, καὶ οὕτως ἀκολούθως ἃ δεῖ πράξομεν.

ἡ δὲ μήτηρ ὑμῶν ἐπειδὴ πιστῶς διάκειται περὶ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, κἂν μίαν πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος νηστευσάτω ἡμέραν. ἡ δὲ ὤμνυεν Δύο τῶν διελθουσῶν ἡμερῶν, τῇ γυναικὶ τὰ κατὰ τὸν ἀναγνωρισμὸν διηγουμένη, ὑπὸ τῆς πολλῆς χαρᾶς τροφῆς μεταλαβεῖν οὐκ ἠδυνήθην ἢ ἐχθὲς μόνον βραχέος ὕδατος. ἐμαρτύρησέ τε τῷ ὅρκῳ ἡ γυνὴ Πέτρου λέγουσα Ἀληθῶς οὐκ ἐγεύσατο. καὶ ὁ Ἀκύλας (μᾶλλον δὲ τοῦ λοιποῦ Φαυστινιανός) ἔφη Οὐκοῦν οὐδὲν κωλύει αὐτὴν βαπτισθῆναι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος γελάσας ἀπεκρίνατο Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστιν τοῦτο νηστεία βαπτίσματος, ἢ μὴ δι’ αὐτὸ γέγονεν. καὶ ὁ Φαυστῖνος ἀπεκρίνατο Ἴσως οὖν ὁ θεὸς βουλόμενος ἡμῶν τὴν μητέρα μηδεμίαν ἡμέραν τῆς ἡμῶν ἐπιγνώσεως χωρίσαι τῆς τραπέζης, προῳκονόμησεν τὴν νηστείαν. ὡς γὰρ ἐσωφρόνησεν ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ, τὸ πρέπον τῆς ἀληθείας ποιήσασα: οὕτως καὶ νῦν ὁ θεὸς ἴσως ᾠκονόμησεν αὐτὴν πρὸ μιᾶς νηστεῦσαι αὐτὴν ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἀληθοῦς βαπτίσματος, ἵνα ἀπὸ πρώτης ἡμέρας τοῦ γνωρίσαι ἡμᾶς σὺν ἡμῖν ἁλῶν μεταλαβεῖν δυνηθῇ.
