  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.

passages.text: Peter said, “You did these things as you had planned. But as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?” My father said, “I will not lie to you: I was genuinely affirming natal destiny as something that exists. For I am not uninitiated in the theory. Besides, there was also with me an Egyptian man named Annubion, best among astrologers. He became my friend at the beginning of my travels and declared the death of my wife along with our children.” Peter said, “Then are you now convinced by what has happened that the claims concerning natal destiny do not hold together?” My father answered, “I must set before you everything that comes into my mind, so that, hearing answers to these things, I can learn by these [points] of this refutation. I know that astrologers are wrong about many things but also tell the truth about many. So I suspect that, in what they determine accurately, they tell the truth, whereas, in what they get wrong, they do so through ignorance. Thus I suppose the discipline itself holds together, but they say false things through ignorance because not everyone can determine everything accurately.” Peter answered, “Hold back: perhaps in the things about which they tell the truth, they happen to hit upon it rather than speaking from precise knowledge. For some of the many things said are bound to come about.” The old man said, “How, then, can one become fully convinced about this: whether what concerns natal destiny holds together or not?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ δὲ γενέσεως ἄρα ψευδόμενος διισχυρίζου· ἢ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἐβεβαίους;
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two alternatives are both retained. ὡς ἀληθεύων can concern the speaker’s sincere claim to truth as well as actual truth; the father’s answer distinguishes sincerity from the theory’s validity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: So I suspect that
lexical_decisions.rationale: The particle marks a tentative possibility or concern; the ensuing contrast is framed as a suspicion, not asserted as established astrological science.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hold back: perhaps
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπεχε can be a caution to pause or refrain. “Consider whether perhaps” is a contextual alternative, but the main text retains the imperative’s restraint rather than treating the matter as proved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: best among astrologers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative superlative ranks Annubion as best among astrologers without adding “the only” or requiring that no one shares that rank. Merely placing him among a group of the best would weaken the source’s wording. An elative “an exceptionally good astrologer” is possible for this adjective, but the explicit plural genitive supports the relative main reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν λεγομένων ἀποβαίνειν τινά.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For some of the many things said are bound to come about
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποβαίνειν here denotes predictions coming about or proving fulfilled. “Come about” makes that result clear without adding a separate causal mechanism or claiming that all predictions succeed.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὰ ἀκούων μανθάνειν ἔχω τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου
source_issues.issue: The sequence τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου is syntactically compressed: τοῖσδε is dative plural while “of this refutation” is genitive singular. The main text supplies only a bracketed generic head, “[points],” taking the dative instrumentally and the genitive as qualifying those implied points: learning by these points of this refutation while hearing replies to the doubts. Another contextual reading would refer to means or stages of refutation rather than particular points. The wording is not emended into a dative plural noun or described as an OCR error. The referential details remain uncertain and require independent review.

passages.text: While both were silent, I said, “Since I know the discipline precisely, but my master and my father do not know it in the same way, I would like, if Annubion himself were present, to hold a discussion in my father’s presence. For then the matter could become clear, with an expert holding the inquiry with another expert in the same field.” My father answered, “Where, then, can Annubion be encountered?” Peter said, “In Antioch. For I learn that Simon the magician is there, and Annubion, who follows him, is inseparable from him. So, when we get there, if we actually find them, the inquiry can take place.” And after we had talked together at length, filled with joy at the recognition and giving thanks to God, we turned to sleep when evening overtook us.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my master
lexical_decisions.rationale: This refers to Peter in the ongoing discussion, not a newly introduced speech of the divine Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an expert ... with another expert in the same field
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same-field relation is explicit; the translation does not certify the underlying astrological discipline as true.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if we actually find them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional prevents the planned inquiry from being reported as already conducted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And after we had talked together at length
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ὁμῶς gives the collective sense, together or in common; πολλὰ supplies the extent of their discussion. Both are preserved. The unfamiliar adverb is neither silently replaced by ὅμως nor characterized as an OCR error.

passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ταῦτα μὲν ἐποίησας ὡς ἐβουλεύσω, περὶ δὲ γενέσεως ἄρα ψευδόμενος διισχυρίζου· ἢ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἐβεβαίους; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἔφη Οὐ ψεύσομαι πρὸς σέ, ἀληθῶς ὡς οὔσης γενέσεως ἐβεβαίουν. εἰμὶ γὰρ οὐκ ἀμύητος τοῦ θεωρήματος, πλὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ συνῆν μοι τίς, ἀστρολόγων ἄριστος, ἀνὴρ αἰγύπτιος, Ἀννουβίων ὀνόματι, ὅστις ἐν ταῖς ἀποδημίαις κατ᾽ ἀρχάς μοι φιλωθεὶς τὸν τῆς ἐμῆς συμβίου μετὰ τῶν τέκνων θάνατον ἐδήλου. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Οὐκοῦν ἔργῳ πέπεισαι νῦν ὅτι οὐ συνέστηκεν τὰ κατὰ γένεσιν; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπεκρίνατο Ἀνάγκη με πάντα τὰ ὑποτρέχοντά μου εἰς τὸν νοῦν ἐκτίθεσθαί σοι, ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὰ ἀκούων μανθάνειν ἔχω τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου. ἀλλὰ καὶ πολλὰ πταίειν οἶδα τοὺς ἀστρολόγους, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἀληθεύειν. ὑποπτεύω οὖν μήπως ἃ μὲν ἀκριβοῦσιν, ἀληθεύουσιν, ἃ δὲ πταίουσιν, ἀμαθίᾳ πάσχουσιν, ὡς ὑπονοεῖν με τὸ μὲν μάθημα συνεστάναι, αὐτοὺς δὲ δι᾽ ἀμαθίαν ψεύδεσθαι διὰ τὸ μὴ πάντας περὶ πάντων ἀκριβοῦν δύνασθαι. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Ἄπεχε μήπως περὶ ὧν ἀληθεύουσιν, ἐπιτυγχάνουσιν καὶ οὐχὶ ἀκριβοῦντες λέγουσιν. ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν λεγομένων ἀποβαίνειν τινά. καὶ ὁ γέρων ἔφη Πῶς οὖν ἐστιν περὶ τούτου πληροφορηθῆναι, τὸ εἴτε συνέστηκεν τὸ κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν ἢ οὔ;

ἀμφοτέρων οὖν σιωπώντων ἔφην ἐγὼ Ἐπειδὴ τὸ μάθημα ἀκριβῶς ἐπίσταμαι, ὁ δὲ κύριος καὶ ὁ πατὴρ οὐχ οὕτως, ἤθελον, εἰ αὐτὸς Ἀννουβίων παρῆν, καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ποιήσασθαι λόγον. οὕτω γὰρ ἂν τὸ πρᾶγμα εἰς φανερὸν ἐλθεῖν ἠδύνατο, τεχνίτου πρὸς ὁμότεχνον τὴν ζήτησιν ἐσχηκότος. καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπεκρίνατο Ποῦ οὖν δυνατόν ἐστιν Ἀννουβίων συντυχεῖν; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ· ἐκεῖ γὰρ μανθάνω Σίμωνα τὸν μάγον ὄντα, ᾧ Ἀννουβίων παρεπόμενος ἀχώριστός ἐστιν. ὡς ἂν οὖν ἐκεῖ γενώμεθα, ἐάν γε καταλάβωμεν αὐτούς, ἡ ζήτησις γενέσθαι δύναται. καὶ ὁμῶς πολλὰ διαλεχθέντες καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ ἀναγνωρισμῷ χαρᾶς πληρωθέντες καὶ θεῷ εὐχαριστήσαντες, ἑσπέρας ἐπικαταλαβούσης εἰς ὕπνον ἐτράπημεν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

passages.text: Peter said, “You did these things as you had planned. But as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?” My father said, “I will not lie to you: I was genuinely affirming natal destiny as something that exists. For I am not uninitiated in the theory. Besides, there was also with me an Egyptian man named Annubion, best among astrologers. He became my friend at the beginning of my travels and declared the death of my wife along with our children.” Peter said, “Then are you now convinced by what has happened that the claims concerning natal destiny do not hold together?” My father answered, “I must set before you everything that comes into my mind, so that, hearing answers to these things, I can learn by these [points] of this refutation. I know that astrologers are wrong about many things but also tell the truth about many. So I suspect that, in what they determine accurately, they tell the truth, whereas, in what they get wrong, they do so through ignorance. Thus I suppose the discipline itself holds together, but they say false things through ignorance because not everyone can determine everything accurately.” Peter answered, “Hold back: perhaps in the things about which they tell the truth, they happen to hit upon it rather than speaking from precise knowledge. For some of the many things said are bound to come about.” The old man said, “How, then, can one become fully convinced about this: whether what concerns natal destiny holds together or not?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ δὲ γενέσεως ἄρα ψευδόμενος διισχυρίζου· ἢ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἐβεβαίους;
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two alternatives are both retained. ὡς ἀληθεύων can concern the speaker’s sincere claim to truth as well as actual truth; the father’s answer distinguishes sincerity from the theory’s validity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: So I suspect that
lexical_decisions.rationale: The particle marks a tentative possibility or concern; the ensuing contrast is framed as a suspicion, not asserted as established astrological science.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hold back: perhaps
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπεχε can be a caution to pause or refrain. “Consider whether perhaps” is a contextual alternative, but the main text retains the imperative’s restraint rather than treating the matter as proved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: best among astrologers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative superlative ranks Annubion as best among astrologers without adding “the only” or requiring that no one shares that rank. Merely placing him among a group of the best would weaken the source’s wording. An elative “an exceptionally good astrologer” is possible for this adjective, but the explicit plural genitive supports the relative main reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν λεγομένων ἀποβαίνειν τινά.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For some of the many things said are bound to come about
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποβαίνειν here denotes predictions coming about or proving fulfilled. “Come about” makes that result clear without adding a separate causal mechanism or claiming that all predictions succeed.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὰ ἀκούων μανθάνειν ἔχω τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου
source_issues.issue: The sequence τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου is syntactically compressed: τοῖσδε is dative plural while “of this refutation” is genitive singular. The main text supplies only a bracketed generic head, “[points],” taking the dative instrumentally and the genitive as qualifying those implied points: learning by these points of this refutation while hearing replies to the doubts. Another contextual reading would refer to means or stages of refutation rather than particular points. The wording is not emended into a dative plural noun or described as an OCR error. The referential details remain uncertain and require independent review.

passages.text: While both were silent, I said, “Since I know the discipline precisely, but my master and my father do not know it in the same way, I would like, if Annubion himself were present, to hold a discussion in my father’s presence. For then the matter could become clear, with an expert holding the inquiry with another expert in the same field.” My father answered, “Where, then, can Annubion be encountered?” Peter said, “In Antioch. For I learn that Simon the magician is there, and Annubion, who follows him, is inseparable from him. So, when we get there, if we actually find them, the inquiry can take place.” And after we had talked together at length, filled with joy at the recognition and giving thanks to God, we turned to sleep when evening overtook us.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my master
lexical_decisions.rationale: This refers to Peter in the ongoing discussion, not a newly introduced speech of the divine Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an expert ... with another expert in the same field
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same-field relation is explicit; the translation does not certify the underlying astrological discipline as true.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if we actually find them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional prevents the planned inquiry from being reported as already conducted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And after we had talked together at length
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ὁμῶς gives the collective sense, together or in common; πολλὰ supplies the extent of their discussion. Both are preserved. The unfamiliar adverb is neither silently replaced by ὅμως nor characterized as an OCR error.

"confirmed_print_features": [], "translation_policy_text": "# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,

  retroactively edited.

passages.text: When dawn came, our father went in with our mother and the three sons to where Peter was. He greeted him and sat down; then we too sat down at Peter's bidding. Looking directly at our father, Peter said, ‘I am eager for you to become of one mind with your wife and children, so that you may share their way of life here and, there too, after the soul's separation from the body, be with them free from sorrow. Or does not your being apart from one another cause the greatest distress to both you and them?’ Our father answered, ‘Very much indeed.’ Peter said, ‘If being separated from one another distresses you even here, since after death you are certainly bound not to be together, will it not distress you much more—you, a wise man, being separated from your family because of your opinion, and them suffering still more in knowing that eternal punishment awaits you for thinking otherwise, by the pronouncement of an explicit decree?’

lexical_decisions.chosen: you to become of one mind with your wife and children
lexical_decisions.rationale: The desired agreement concerns their beliefs in the ensuing discussion; it is not reduced to living at the same address or expanded into agreement on every possible matter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ θάνατον πάντως ὀφειλόμενον ὑμῖν μετ’ ἀλλήλων μὴ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: since after death you are certainly bound not to be together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause states the anticipated separation emphatically within Peter's warning. Its connection to the father's different beliefs is supplied by the surrounding explicit clauses, not by removing the source's certainty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the pronouncement of an explicit decree
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive adjective can mean expressly stated or definite. Decree or ordinance preserves the authoritative ruling; the source does not identify a particular quoted verse or name its speaker here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘But, dearest friend, souls are not punished in Hades, since the soul dissolves into air as soon as it leaves the body.’ Peter said, ‘Until we persuade you about this, then, answer me: does it not seem to you that, while you do not suffer distress because you disbelieve in punishment, they, being convinced of it, must be troubled about you?’ Our father said, ‘Your argument follows.’ Peter said, ‘Why, then, will you not relieve them of their very great sorrow about you by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment, listening to what I tell you and judging whether it is so or not. If things are as we say, you will share enjoyment with your dearest ones here and share their rest there. But if, in examining your arguments, you show that what we say is a false myth, you will do well even so: having brought them to your own way of thinking, you will stop them from relying on empty hopes and free them from false fears.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ θρησκείᾳ συνθέμενος, οὐ δυσωπίᾳ λέγω, ἀλλ’ εὐγνωμοσύνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: Θρησκεία concerns religious observance or worship; our is inferred from Peter's invitation. Δυσωπία can denote shamefaced compliance or reluctance to disappoint, contrasted with sound judgment rather than mere social acquiescence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῇ τῶν λόγων σου σκέψει
lexical_decisions.chosen: in examining your arguments
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive your is retained rather than silently changed to our. The father's own examination or examination of his arguments can both be heard in the genitive construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: share their rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future middle addresses the father and continues the togetherness expressed by the preceding compound. Rest is retained without adding a location or detailed doctrine of the afterlife not given here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You seem to me to be saying many reasonable things.’ Peter said, ‘Tell me, then, what is holding you back from coming to our faith, so that we may begin to speak directly to it. There are many things that hold people back. For those already convinced, there are the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties, and things of that sort. For unbelievers, among whom you too belong, there are assumptions: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist, or that everything is subject to birth-fate or to chance, or that souls are mortal, or that our message is false because there is no providence.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: everything is subject to birth-fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Genesis here can denote the determining configuration or fate associated with birth, as distinguished from chance in the next alternative. Birth-fate keeps the birth wording visible; fate determined by the stars at birth is a fuller contextual alternative, but stars are not expressly named in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: chance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to spontaneous occurrence without directing providence. It is not rendered automation, a misleading modern technical association.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural occupations or lack of leisure is the governing idea, and all four listed sources of preoccupation are retained.

passages.text: ‘But I say that everything is governed by God's providence, judging from what has happened to you: your separation from your family for so many years. Since, if they had remained with you, perhaps they would not have listened to the teachings of reverence for God, their journey abroad with their mother was arranged, along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact. So too was their education in Greek and godless doctrines, so that, knowing them, they might be better able to refute them. After this came their love for the teaching of reverence for God and their ability to join me in helping my proclamation; then their brother Clement's coming together with us, and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing. Shortly afterward came the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn, and, on the following day, meeting you and your recovering your family. I do not think that so swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact
lexical_decisions.rationale: The list describes the circumstances of the family separation. Ἀπαρτία is read as absence of news or contact in this context; the translation does not supply a particular duration beyond the previously stated years.

lexical_decisions.chosen: becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The mother continues as the inferred person receiving assurance. Θεότης is divinity or divine nature, whose precise referent the clause leaves unnamed; this is not translated as an assertion that the mother herself became divine or that Peter was a god.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both passive and active recognition are retained. The unexpressed object of their recognition is not replaced by an invented named person in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: upon one intended aim
lexical_decisions.rationale: The convergence is toward one aim of intention or purpose. Agreement of belief is a possible contextual emphasis for γνώμη, but the preceding arrangement of events favors an intended aim without naming a separate planner in this phrase.

passages.text: Our father began to say to Peter, ‘Do not suppose, my dearest Peter, that I have not been thinking about the message you proclaim. Indeed, at the end of this past night, when Clement urged me at length to agree with the truth you proclaim, I answered, “What newer instruction can anyone give beyond what the ancients advised?” He smiled gently and said, “There is a great difference, father, between the teachings of reverence for God and those of philosophy. For the message of truth has its proof from prophecy, whereas the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures.” Having said this, however, he set out for me, as an example, the teaching about love for humanity that you had explained to him. It seemed to me, rather, utterly unjust. I will tell you how. He said that it was just for someone to offer the other cheek as well to the person striking his cheek; to give his head-covering too to the person taking his cloak; to go two miles with the person compelling him to go one; and other things of this sort.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The favorable-sounding language and the qualification seems are retained alongside the criticism of conjectural proofs. The translation does not replace conjecture by observation or prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he set out for me ... the teaching about love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term is a broad humane love or kindness toward human beings. Love for humanity keeps its human object explicit and connects it with the ensuing discussion of humane treatment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his head-covering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The garment can be a scarf, kerchief, or head-covering. It is distinguished from the cloak named immediately before it, rather than replaced by the tunic familiar from another form of the saying.

generation_provenance.method: Fresh translation directly from supplied checked Greek
generation_provenance.authorization: Zack directly approved Codex translators for provider-filtered and remaining unstarted passages; keep live Azure calls intact and require separate Sol6.1 source review

findings.source_quote: ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι
findings.english_quote: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist
findings.issue: The existential rendering is defensible, but the notes do not disclose the alternative predicative construction: considering those who are not gods to be gods. The alternatives distinguish denying the supposed gods' existence from denying the divinity of beings treated as gods.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note preserving the alternative ‘thinking that those who are not gods are gods’ and explaining why the main text takes τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας existentially. The present main rendering need not be rejected merely because this alternative exists.

findings.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι
findings.english_quote: and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
findings.issue: The draft continues the mother as the subject of πληροφορηθῆναι and takes τὴν θεότητα as the content of her conviction. That is a defensible interpretation, but the note discusses only the unnamed referent of ‘divinity’. It omits the material syntactic alternative in which τὴν θεότητα is the accusative subject of the second passive infinitive: the divinity or divine power was fully confirmed through healing.
findings.suggested_revision: Expand the note to distinguish the two constructions explicitly. If retaining the main text, explain the inferred continuation of the mother as subject and the accusative of content. Preserve the alternative ‘and the divinity was fully confirmed through healing’, supported by the parallel accusative subjects of the passive infinitives. Do not identify whose divinity is meant without further support.

findings.source_quote: τοσαύτην οὖν ταχεῖαν ἁρμονίαν
findings.english_quote: so swift a harmony
findings.issue: The English collapses the magnitude expressed by τοσαύτην into the degree of speed expressed by ταχεῖαν. The Greek separately characterizes the harmony as so great and swift.
findings.suggested_revision: Render the conclusion along the lines of ‘I therefore do not think that so great and swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’ This proposed wording requires fresh review before acceptance.

findings.source_quote: καὶ ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπὼν
findings.english_quote: Having said this, however,
findings.issue: The contextual adversative rendering is defensible, but the supplied print reads ὁμῶς, not the usual adversative spelling ὅμως. The notes do not disclose this accentual and lexical feature or distinguish the adversative interpretation from the non-adversative senses ‘alike’ or ‘together’. This is not evidence of OCR corruption and does not require renewed print verification.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a source-quoted note retaining ὁμῶς exactly, explaining its adversative interpretation here and acknowledging the non-adversative lexical alternative. Distinguish that interpretation from any proposed normalization to ὅμως; do not silently change the supplied Greek.

passages.source_text: Ὄρθρου δὲ γενομένου ὁ πατὴρ μετὰ τῆς μητρὸς ἡμῶν καὶ τῶν τριῶν υἱῶν εἰσελθὼν ἔνθα ὁ Πέτρος ἦν, προσαγορεύσας ἐκαθέσθη, ἔπειτα καὶ ἡμεῖς, αὐτοῦ κελεύσαντος. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος τῷ πατρὶ προσεμβλέψας ἔφη Σπεύδω ὁμόφρονά σε γενέσθαι γυναικὶ καὶ τέκνοις, ὅπως αὐτοῖς καὶ ἐνταῦθα ὁμοδίαιτος ᾖς κἀκεῖ μετὰ τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος τῆς ψυχῆς χωρισμὸν συνὼν ἄλυπος ἔσῃ. ἢ γὰρ οὐ τὰ μέγιστα σὲ λυπεῖ καὶ αὐτοὺς τὸ μὴ ἀλλήλοις συνεῖναι; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Καὶ πάνυ γε. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Εἰ οὖν καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὸ ἀλλήλων κεχωρίσθαι λυπεῖ, μετὰ θάνατον πάντως ὀφειλόμενον ὑμῖν μετ’ ἀλλήλων μὴ εἶναι: πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον οὐ λυπήσει σὲ μὲν ἄνδρα σοφὸν ὄντα τῷ τῆς γνώμης λόγῳ σου τῶν σῶν κεχωρίσθαι, αὐτοὺς δὲ πολὺ μᾶλλον ὀδυνᾶσθαι τῷ εἰδέναι, ὅτι σε ἄλλα φρονοῦντα αἰώνιος μένει κόλασις, ῥητοῦ δόγματος ἀποφάσει;

καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἔφη Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστιν, ὦ φίλτατε, τὸ ἐν ᾅδου ψυχὰς κολάζεσθαι, αὐτῆς ἅμα τῷ ἀποστῆναι τοῦ σώματος εἰς ἀέρα λυομένης. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Μέχρις οὖν ὅτε ἂν περὶ τούτου πείσωμέν σε (ἀπόκριναί μοι) οὐ δοκεῖ σοι σὲ μὲν ἀπιστοῦντα τὴν κόλασιν μὴ λυπεῖσθαι, ἐκείνους δὲ πεπεισμένους ἀνάγκην ἔχειν περὶ σοῦ ἀνιᾶσθαι; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Ἀκολούθως λέγεις. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Διὰ τί δὲ αὐτοὺς οὐκ ἀπαλλάξεις μεγίστης περὶ σοῦ λύπης τῇ θρησκείᾳ συνθέμενος, οὐ δυσωπίᾳ λέγω, ἀλλ’ εὐγνωμοσύνῃ, περὶ τῶν λεγομένων σοι ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ ἀκούων καὶ κρίνων εἰ ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει ἢ οὔ; καὶ εἰ μὲν οὕτως ἔχει ὡς λέγομεν: καὶ ὧδε συναπολαύσεις τοῖς φιλτάτοις κἀκεῖ συναναπαύσει· εἰ δὲ ἐν τῇ τῶν λόγων σου σκέψει δείξῃς τὰ ὑφ’ ἡμῶν λεγόμενα μῦθόν τινα ψευδῆ εἶναι: καὶ οὕτως καλῶς ποιήσεις, αὐτοὺς ὁμογνώμονάς σοι εἰληφὼς, καὶ τοῦ κεναῖς ἐλπίσιν ἐπερείδεσθαι παύσεις καὶ ψευδῶν φόβων ἀπαλλάξεις.

καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Πολλὰ φαίνῃ μοι εὔλογα λέγων. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Τί οὖν ἔστιν τὸ κρατοῦν σε μὴ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν πίστιν ἐλθεῖν, λέγε, ἵνα εἰς αὐτὸ λέγειν ἀρξώμεθα. πολλὰ γάρ ἐστιν τὰ κρατοῦντα· τοὺς μὲν πεπεισμένους ἀσχολίαι ἀγορασμῶν, πράξεων, γεωργιῶν, φροντίδων καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα· ἀπιστοῦσι δὲ (ἀφ’ ὧν εἶ καὶ σύ) ὑπολήψεις τοῦ νομίζειν ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι ἢ τὸ γενέσει τὰ πάντα ὑποκεῖσθαι ἢ αὐτοματισμῷ ἢ τὰς ψυχὰς θνητὰς ἢ καὶ τὸν ἡμέτερον λόγον ψευδῆ ὡς οὐκ οὔσης προνοίας.

ἐγὼ δὲ προνοίᾳ θεοῦ τὰ πάντα διοικεῖσθαι ἐκ τῶν περὶ σὲ γενομένων εἶναι λέγω, τοῦ τοσούτοις ἔτεσιν τὴν διάστασιν σοῦ τε καὶ τῶν σῶν γενέσθαι. ἐπεὶ γὰρ σὺν σοὶ ὄντες ἴσως τῶν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγων οὐκ ἂν ἐπήκουσαν, ᾠκονομήθη σὺν μητρὶ ἡ ἀποδημία καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ, ἔτι τε καὶ ἐκπαιδευθῆναι αὐτοὺς τὰ Ἑλλήνων καὶ ἄθεα δόγματα, ἵνα μᾶλλον ὡς εἰδότες ταῦτα ἀνασκευάζειν δυνατοὶ ὦσιν — ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ φιλῆσαι τὸν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγον καὶ ἐμοὶ ἑνωθῆναι δυνηθῆναι πρὸς τὸ συλλαβέσθαι μου τῷ κηρύγματι — ἀλλ’ ἔτι μὴν συνελθεῖν καὶ τὸν ἀδελφὸν Κλήμεντα καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι — καὶ μετ’ οὐ πολὺ εὐθὺ τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα καὶ τῆς ἄλλης ἡμέρας σοὶ συντυχεῖν καὶ τοὺς σοὺς ἀπολαβεῖν. τοσαύτην οὖν ταχεῖαν ἁρμονίαν πανταχόθεν συνδραμοῦσαν εἰς ἕνα γνώμης σκοπὸν οὐκ οἶμαι ἀπρονόητον εἶναι.

καὶ ὁ πατὴρ τῷ Πέτρῳ ἤρξατο λέγειν Μὴ νόμιζε, φίλτατέ μοι Πέτρε, ἐν ἐννοίᾳ μὴ ἔχειν περὶ τοῦ ὑπὸ σοῦ κηρυσσομένου λόγου. πέρας γοῦν ταύτης τῆς παρῳχηκυίας νυκτὸς πολλὰ τοῦ Κλήμεντος προτρεπομένου με τῇ ὑπὸ σοῦ κηρυσσομένῃ ἀληθείᾳ συνθέσθαι, ἀπεκρινάμην Τί γὰρ καινότερον ἐντέλλεσθαι δύναταί τις παρ’ ὃ οἱ ἀρχαῖοι παρῄνεσαν; ὁ δὲ ἠρέμα γελάσας ἔφη Πολλὴ διαφορά, πάτερ, μεταξὺ τῶν τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγων καὶ τῶν τῆς φιλοσοφίας. ὁ γὰρ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγος ἀπόδειξιν ἔχει τὴν ἐκ προφητείας, ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις. καὶ ὁμῶς ταῦτα εἰπὼν δείγματος χάριν τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον, ὅνπερ αὐτῷ ὑφηγήσω, ὃς ἀδικώτατός μοι μᾶλλον ἐφαίνετο. καὶ τὸ πῶς ἐρῶ. δίκαιον ἔφασκεν εἶναι καὶ τῷ τύπτοντι αὐτοῦ τὴν σιαγόνα παρατιθέναι καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν, καὶ τῷ αἴροντι αὐτοῦ τὸ ἱμάτιον προσδιδόναι καὶ τὸ μαφόριον, ἀγγαρεύοντι δὲ μίλιον ἓν συναπέρχεσθαι δύο, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
