Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. Those who fashioned you appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who fashioned you appear to be two
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fashioned repeats the preceding πλάσαντός, preserving Simon's shared wording and its distinction from make in the quotation. You is understood from the preceding God who fashioned you, rather than identifying an additional created object not in the context.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall surely know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tempter was testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The agent is a substantivized participle, the one who tests or tempts, not a separately supplied Greek noun. The main English varies the lexical roots as tempter and testing; it does not reproduce the Greek's repeated root. A neutral, root-transparent alternative is the one who tests was testing, or the tester was testing. Tempter is chosen because the preceding act tempts toward apostasy and Peter argues against identifying the agent with an omniscient God who needs to learn. The neutral testing interpretation remains a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked print places a middle dot immediately before γραφῶν. The English translates the surviving wording without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected, no wording restored, and no OCR error or established lacuna is inferred from this apparent print feature.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: angels have been called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. Also preserves the additive καὶ but does not by itself establish other sons. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves that pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving its antecedent silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes from the scriptures as identifying the source material in which false things are recognized. The following contrast with the scriptures' true things supports this material-source reading. A material alternative attaches the phrase to recognition as its evidentiary basis: In obedience to him, we recognize what is false from the scriptures, meaning by scriptural evidence. Neither attachment is claimed to be uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering understands the neuter phrase ἀληθὲς ὂν as characterizing the preceding assertion about the one creator, while masculine τοῦτον identifies the God handed on. A material alternative takes ὂν substantivally as being: having affirmed this one as a true being through God-loving reasoning, the fathers handed him on to us. The supplied gender distinction is retained and disclosed, not corrected or diagnosed as OCR corruption.

source_issues.issue: The selected print has a point immediately before δὲ. The English translates the surviving words as a continuous construction, without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected or missing wording restored; the apparent print feature is not labeled an OCR error or an established lacuna.

passages.source_text: καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἀπεκρίνατο Μή με βιάζου ἀκρίτως συνθέσθαι σοι, ἵνα δόξω φιλαλήθης εἶναι κριτής· εἰ δὲ τἀληθῆ ἀκοῦσαι θέλεις, τῷ σῷ φρονήματι μᾶλλον προείλημμαι. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Πῶς προείληψαι, οὐκ εἰδὼς ὃ φρονῶ; καὶ ὁ πατὴρ Τοῦτο ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν εἰδέναι· καὶ πῶς, ἄκουσον. ἐλέγξειν ὑπέσχου Πέτρον ἕνα θεὸν λέγοντα εἶναι ὅτι ψεύδεται, ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος πάντως εὔδηλον ὡς ἐκεῖνος ἀληθεύων οὐ τὸ αὐτὸ λέγει. εἰ γὰρ τῷ καταψευδομένῳ τὸ αὐτὸ λέγει, καὶ αὐτὸς ψεύδεται· εἰ δὲ τὰ ἐναντία λέγων ἀποδείκνυσιν, τότε ἀληθεύει. οὐκ ἄλλως οὖν τὸν ἕνα θεὸν εἶναι λέγοντα ψεύστην λέγεις, εἰ μήτι ἂν ὅτι πολλοὺς δοξάζεις θεούς. θεοὺς δὲ πολλοὺς εἶναι κἀγὼ λέγω. τὸ αὐτὸ οὖν σοι πρὸ τῆς ζητήσεως λέγων σοι μᾶλλον προείλημμαι. καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἀγωνιᾶν περὶ ἐμοῦ οὐκ ὀφείλεις, ἀλλὰ Πέτρος, ὅτι ἀκμὴν αὐτῷ τὰ ἐναντία φρονῶ, ὅσπερ μετὰ τὴν ὑμετέραν ζήτησιν ἐλπίζω φιλαλήθης ὢν κριτής, πρόληψιν ἀποδυσάμενος, τῷ ἐπικρατοῦντι συνθέσθαι λόγῳ. ταῦτα τοῦ πατρὸς εἰπόντος ἠρέμα βοή τις ἐπαίνου ἐκ τῶν ὄχλων ἐγένετο ἐπὶ τῷ οὕτως τὸν πατέρα διαλεχθῆναι.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἐπεὶ πυκνότερόν σε ὁρῶ τὸν λόγον ποιούμενον ὑπὲρ τοῦ πλάσαντός σε θεοῦ, μάθε παρ’ ἐμοῦ πῶς καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἀσεβεῖς. οἱ πλάσαντες δύο φαίνονται ὡς ἡ γραφὴ λέγει „καὶ εἶπεν ὁ θεὸς Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν“. τὸ „ποιήσωμεν“ δύο σημαίνει ἢ πλείονας, πλὴν οὐχ ἕνα.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἀπεκρίνατο Εἴτε αἱ γραφαὶ εἴτε προφῆται θεοὺς λέγουσιν, εἰς πειρασμὸν τῶν ἀκουόντων λέγουσιν. οὕτω γὰρ γέγραπται· „ἐὰν ἀναστῇ ἐν σοὶ προφήτης, διδοὺς σοι σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα, καὶ ἔλθῃ τό τε σημεῖον ἐκεῖνο τό τε τέρας, ἐρεῖ δέ σοι Πορευθέντες λατρεύσωμεν θεοῖς ἑτέροις, οἷς οὐκ ᾔδεισαν οἱ πατέρες σου: οὐκ ἀκούσεσθε τοῦ προφήτου ἐκείνου· ἐν πρώτοις ἔστωσαν αἱ χεῖρές σου λιθοβολῆσαι αὐτόν. ἐπείρασεν γάρ σε ἀποστῆναι ἀπὸ κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου. ἐὰν δὲ εἴπῃς ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ σου Πῶς ἐποίησεν τὸ σημεῖον ἐκεῖνο ἢ τὸ τέρας: γινώσκων γνώσῃ ὅτι ὁ πειράζων ἐπείραζεν ἰδεῖν εἰ φοβῇ κύριον τὸν θεόν σου“. ὅτι δὲ ὁ πειράζων ἐπείραζεν, εἴρητο, ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται. οὐ γὰρ ἂν ὁ τὰ πάντα γινώσκων θεὸς (ὡς ἐκ πολλῶν ἔστιν δεῖξαι) ἐπείραζεν, ἵνα γνῷ αὐτός, ὁ τὰ πάντα προγινώσκων. εἰ δὲ βούλει, περὶ τούτου τὸν λόγον ποιησόμεθα, καὶ δείξω προγινώσκοντα τὸν θεόν. τὸ δὲ ἀγνοεῖν αὐτὸν ψεῦσμα ὂν καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς πειρασμὸν γραφὲν ἀποδέδεικται. οὕτως ἡμεῖς, ὦ Σίμων, οὔτε ἀπὸ ·γραφῶν οὔτε ὑφ’ ἑτέρου τινὸς σκανδαλισθῆναι δυνάμεθα οὔτε πολλοὺς θεοὺς ἀποδέξασθαι ἀπατώμεθα οὐδὲ λόγῳ τινὶ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ λεγομένῳ συντιθέμεθα.

ἴσμεν γὰρ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν ἀγγέλους θεοὺς λεχθέντας, λέγω δὲ ὡς ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸν γεννώμενον Ἐμμανουὴλ καὶ τὸν λεγόμενον θεὸν ἰσχυρόν. ἀλλὰ μὴν καὶ Μωϋσῆς θεὸς Φαραὼ ἐγενήθη, τῷ δὲ ὄντι ἄνθρωπος ἦν. ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ εἴδωλα τῶν ἐθνῶν. ἡμῖν δὲ εἷς θεός, εἷς· ὁ τὰς κτίσεις πεποιηκὼς καὶ διακοσμήσας τὰ πάντα, οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν. ἔτι .δὲ καὶ ἐκ πατέρων ἐφοδιαζόμενοι τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ἀληθῆ ἕνα μόνον οἴδαμεν τὸν πεποιηκότα τούς τε οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὴν γῆν, θεὸν Ἰουδαίων καὶ πάντων τῶν σέβειν αὐτὸν αἱρουμένων. τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν, ἵνα εἰδῶμεν ὅτι εἴ τι κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ λέγεται, ψεῦδός ἐστιν. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπερβαλλόντως τι ἐρῶ Εἰ τοῦτο οὕτως ὡς ἔφην οὐκ ἔχει, ἐμοὶ γένοιτο καὶ τοῖς τἀληθὲς ἀγαπῶσιν περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,

passages.text: Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same thing as the one speaking falsely, he too is lying. But if he says the opposite and proves it, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I say the same thing as you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one speaking falsely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the participle in a middle sense concerning false speech, since the conditional argument compares two speakers making the same supposedly false assertion. A material passive alternative is the one being falsely accused or lied about. That passive sense does not itself establish the accused person as actually false; neither reading is presented as uncontested, and the conditional remains hypothetical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who has stripped off preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied print has ἐλέξαι. Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. Those who fashioned you appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who fashioned you appear to be two
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fashioned repeats the preceding πλάσαντός, preserving Simon's shared wording and its distinction from make in the quotation. You is understood from the preceding God who fashioned you, rather than identifying an additional created object not in the context.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall surely know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tempter was testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The agent is a substantivized participle, the one who tests or tempts, not a separately supplied Greek noun. The main English varies the lexical roots as tempter and testing; it does not reproduce the Greek's repeated root. A neutral, root-transparent alternative is the one who tests was testing, or the tester was testing. Tempter is chosen because the preceding act tempts toward apostasy and Peter argues against identifying the agent with an omniscient God who needs to learn. The neutral testing interpretation remains a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked print places a middle dot immediately before γραφῶν. The English translates the surviving wording without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected, no wording restored, and no OCR error or established lacuna is inferred from this apparent print feature.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: angels have been called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. Also preserves the additive καὶ but does not by itself establish other sons. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves that pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving its antecedent silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes from the scriptures as identifying the source material in which false things are recognized. The following contrast with the scriptures' true things supports this material-source reading. A material alternative attaches the phrase to recognition as its evidentiary basis: In obedience to him, we recognize what is false from the scriptures, meaning by scriptural evidence. Neither attachment is claimed to be uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering understands the neuter phrase ἀληθὲς ὂν as characterizing the preceding assertion about the one creator, while masculine τοῦτον identifies the God handed on. A material alternative takes ὂν substantivally as being: having affirmed this one as a true being through God-loving reasoning, the fathers handed him on to us. The supplied gender distinction is retained and disclosed, not corrected or diagnosed as OCR corruption.

source_issues.issue: The selected print has a point immediately before δὲ. The English translates the surviving words as a continuous construction, without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected or missing wording restored; the apparent print feature is not labeled an OCR error or an established lacuna.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

passages.text: ‘Indeed, in the law's first utterance he even appears to speak of them as like himself. For it is written that the first human had received God's command to eat from every tree in the garden, but not to eat from the tree of knowing good and evil. The serpent, through the woman, persuaded them to eat on the promise that they would become gods, and caused them to see. Then, when they had come to see, God said to them, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” Thus the serpent, saying, “You will be like gods,” appears to have spoken as though gods exist, all the more so since God too testified, saying, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” So the serpent, who said that there are many gods, did not lie. Again, the writing, “You shall not speak evil of gods, and you shall not speak badly of the rulers of your people,” indicates many gods, of whom he does not even wish evil to be spoken. Elsewhere too it is written, “Has another god dared to go in and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation, as I, the Lord God, have?” In saying, “Has another god dared,” he spoke as though others exist. And elsewhere, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish,” as those who did not make them are going to perish. Somewhere else it says, “Watch yourself, lest you go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,” as though other gods exist, whom he also tells them not to follow. And again, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” Here too he speaks of many gods, whose names he does not wish to be named. Again it is written, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods.” And again, “Who is like you, Lord, among gods?” And again, “God of gods, the Lord.” And again, “God stood in an assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods.” So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify in writing that there are many gods, you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist. For the rest, if you have anything to say in response to these clear statements, speak before everyone.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: caused them to see
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean look up or regain sight. The ensuing Adam quotation and the related form ἀναβλέψασιν support their coming to sight or awareness here; opened their eyes is an idiomatic alternative but supplies an unexpressed anatomical object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the more so since God too testified
lexical_decisions.rationale: The awkward comparative sequence is read as reinforcing the serpent's statement with God's corroboration. More literally, all the more in this respect—or even God testified. The main text makes the evidentiary link intelligible without changing who speaks or testifies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the printed οὐ and the subsequent prohibition's negatives are retained. The resulting question is rhetorically awkward in Simon's argument; the initial negative is not silently deleted or changed into a different Greek word to resolve the difficulty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted Greek title is translated Lord, not replaced by Yahweh, since this is the wording quoted by the ancient author rather than a fresh translation from a Hebrew divine-name occurrence.

source_issues.issue: This wording is supplied within editorial square brackets in the selected edition. The English translates that supplied wording, including the negative and the destruction clause; it is not an independent recovery or proof that the bracketed words survive unbroken in the underlying witness. There is no printed dotted gap here to invent or fill.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Hear a briefer reply to what you have said. The law itself, which has often spoken of gods, itself says to the Jewish multitude, “Look, to the Lord your God belong the heaven of heaven and everything in them.” This includes the point that, even if gods exist, they are under him, that is, under the God of the Jews. Again, “For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.” Somewhere else scripture says to the Jewish multitude, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods,” as though to say that even if gods exist, they are under the God of the Jews. Elsewhere scripture says of him, “The great and true God, who shows no partiality and will accept no gift, rendering justice to orphan and widow.” In calling the God of the Jews great, true, and one who renders justice, scripture indicated that the others are small and not true. Elsewhere too scripture says, “As I live, says the Lord, there is no other god besides me. I am first; I am after these things; besides me there is no god.” Again, “You shall fear the Lord your God and worship him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” Indeed, many utterances seal with an oath that God is one and that there is no god besides him. So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify that there is one God, you say there are many.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the heaven of heaven and everything in them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular heaven of heaven and the ensuing plural pronoun are preserved as quoted, rather than harmonized with a different scriptural form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: shows no partiality and will accept no gift
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first idiom concerns favoritism rather than literally taking a face. The second names a gift in a judicial context, where bribe is a plausible explanatory alternative; the main wording keeps the source's expressed noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am first; I am after these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied expression after these things is translated rather than replaced with the familiar but unprinted title last.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord your God is one Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted word order permits the traditional one-Lord rendering or the Lord is one. The main rendering keeps the repeated Lord and the explicit numerical one, without importing a different creed or Hebrew wording.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods also instructed us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.chosen: also instructed us, saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb presents the scriptures as providing the instruction that follows. They appeared before us is a more spatially literal alternative; the argument treats their quoted prohibition as the operative instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: firmament
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves speak of many gods and at other times of only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.chosen: what must we conclude
lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: mislead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘They do not mislead; they expose, bringing into the open the evil intention against God that lurks like a serpent within each person. For they lie before us resembling many different impressions. Each person, having his own intention like wax, looks over them and finds everything in them. Whatever kind of god he wants to exist, he presses upon them his intention, which, as I said, resembles wax, and takes its impression. Since, then, anyone finds in them whatever he wishes to think about God, one person takes impressions of many gods from them. We, however, have taken the image of the one who truly exists, recognizing the true impression from our own form. Moreover, the soul within us is clothed in his image for immortality. If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment, recognizing me as unjust from that very act of audacity. Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me, and thus I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed. If there is another god, let him first clothe me in another appearance, another form, so that through the body's new form I may recognize the new god. But even if he changes the form, will he also change the soul's substance? If he changes that too, I am no longer myself, having become another in both form and substance. Let him therefore fashion others, if there is another. But there is not. If there were, he would have fashioned them. Since he has not fashioned them, being nonexistent, let him leave the one who truly exists alone. For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone. I accept no other God besides the one who created me.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: impressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The scriptures' differing patterns are likened to forms that stamp wax. Impressions keeps the molding image that develops in the verbs of pressing and taking an imprint; types or models are lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronouns are read as referring to the immediately preceding image in which the soul is clothed. The soul itself is a grammatically possible alternative, but the ensuing loss of assistance and destruction as to the soul favors the protecting image as what departs.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με
lexical_decisions.chosen: Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase from a just one is read as the image's provenance from the righteous creator. A more literal alternative is and, as from a just one, it will justly abandon me; the main text does not make the unjust person just in order to remove the tension.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative soul is taken as the respect in which destruction occurs, and it continues the image as the help's source. This conditional destruction is not softened into bodily death alone or harmonized with the later description of souls as immortal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative concerns the proposed other god. The genitive Simon's completes opinion across the printed punctuation; no second speaker or missing sentence is invented.

findings.source_quote: αὐταὶ παρήγεσαν ἡμῖν εἰποῦσαι
findings.english_quote: also instructed us, saying
findings.issue: The printed παρήγεσαν is a form of παράγω, expressing bringing forward or passing by, rather than directly meaning 'instructed.' The following prohibition certainly functions as instruction, but the draft substitutes that function for the verb's presentation or movement sense. The note acknowledges a spatial alternative without adequately preserving the printed verb in the main wording.
findings.suggested_revision: Use a source-transparent presentation rendering, provisionally 'themselves also brought this before us, saying,' with 'this' referring to the quotation that follows. Revise the note to identify παράγω and distinguish the alternative intransitive reading, 'passed before us.' Neither proposal requires correcting the verified print; the revised wording requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: ἐπεὶ οὖν αὐταὶ αἱ γραφαὶ πολλοὺς λέγουσιν εἶναι θεοὺς καὶ ἄλλοτε ἕνα μόνον εἶναι
findings.english_quote: Since, then, the scriptures themselves speak of many gods and at other times of only one
findings.issue: The Greek explicitly reports assertions of existence: the scriptures say that there are many gods and elsewhere that there is only one. 'Speak of' weakens these assertions into references or mentions. This matters because the passage distinguishes speaking or naming gods from asserting that they exist, and its concluding accusation depends on the conflicting existential assertions.
findings.suggested_revision: Replace this wording with 'Since, then, the scriptures themselves say that there are many gods and at other times that there is only one'. Retain the subsequent contrast concerning speaking evil unchanged, subject to fresh review of the revised passage.

passages.source_text: αὐτίκα γοῦν ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ φωνῇ τοῦ νόμου φαίνεται καὶ ἑαυτῷ αὐτοὺς ὁμοίους λέγων. οὕτως γὰρ γέγραπται ὡς ὅτι τῷ πρώτῳ ἀνθρώπῳ, ἐντολὴν ἔχοντι παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ φαγεῖν, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρὸν μὴ φαγεῖν, ὁ ὄφις διὰ τῆς γυναικὸς ἐπὶ ὑποσχέσει τοῦ γενέσθαι αὐτοὺς θεοὺς φαγεῖν αὐτοὺς πείσας, ἀναβλέψαι ἐποίησεν καὶ εἶθ᾽ οὕτως ὁ θεὸς ἀναβλέψασιν αὐτοῖς ἔφη „ἰδοὺ γέγονεν Ἀδὰμ ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν“. ὁ μὲν οὖν ὄφις εἰπὼν „ἔσεσθε ὡς θεοὶ“ ὡς ὄντων θεῶν εἰρηκὼς φαίνεται ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν εἰπὼν „ἰδοὺ γέγονεν Ἀδὰμ ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν“. οὕτως ὁ τοὺς πολλοὺς εἰπὼν ὄφις εἶναι θεοὺς οὐκ ἐψεύσατο. πάλιν τὸ γεγράφθαι „θεοὺς οὐ κακολογήσεις καὶ ἄρχοντας τοῦ λαοῦ σου οὐ κακῶς ἐρεῖς“ πολλοὺς σημαίνει θεούς, οὓς οὐδὲ κακολογεῖσθαι θέλει. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλοθί που γέγραπται „εἰ ἐτόλμησεν θεὸς ἕτερος εἰσελθεῖν καὶ λαβεῖν ἑαυτῷ ἔθνος ἐκ μέσου ἔθνους ὡς ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεός“. τὸ εἰπεῖν „εἰ ἐτόλμησεν θεὸς ἕτερος“ ὡς ὄντων ἑτέρων εἴρηκεν. καὶ ἄλλοτε „θεοὶ οἳ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν [οὐκ ἐποίησαν, ἀπολέσθωσαν“ ὡς τῶν] μὴ πεποιηκότων ἀπόλλυσθαι μελλόντων. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει „ἔπεχε σεαυτῷ, μὴ πορευθεὶς λατρεύσῃς θεοῖς ἑτέροις, οἷς οὐκ ᾔδεισαν οἱ πατέρες σου“, ὡς ὄντων θεῶν ἑτέρων, οἷς καὶ μὴ ἐξακολουθεῖν αὐτοὺς λέγει. καὶ πάλιν „ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων οὐκ ἀναβήσεται ἐπὶ τῶν χειλέων σου“. καὶ ἐνταῦθα πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγει, ὧν τὰ ὀνόματα ὀνομάζεσθαι οὐ θέλει. καὶ πάλιν γέγραπται „κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς τῶν θεῶν“. καὶ πάλιν „τίς ὅμοιός σοι, κύριε, ἐν θεοῖς;“ καὶ πάλιν „θεὸς θεῶν κύριος“. καὶ πάλιν „ὁ θεὸς ἔστη ἐν συναγωγῇ θεῶν, ἐν μέσῳ δὲ θεοὺς διακρίνει“. ὅθεν θαυμάζω πῶς τοσούτων φωνῶν ἐγγράφως μαρτυρουσῶν πολλοὺς εἶναι θεούς, οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν. λοιπὸν πρὸς τὰ σαφῶς ῥηθέντα εἴ τι ἔχεις εἰπεῖν, ἐπὶ πάντων λέγε.

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Συντομώτερον ἄκουε πρὸς ἃ εἴρηκας. αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος ὁ πολλάκις εἰπὼν θεοὺς αὐτὸς τῷ Ἰουδαίῳ ὄχλῳ λέγει „ἰδοὺ κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς“, συνπεριλαβὼν ὅτι εἰ καὶ εἰσὶν θεοί, ὑπ’ αὐτόν εἰσιν, τουτέστιν ὑπὸ τὸν Ἰουδαίων θεόν. καὶ πάλιν „ὅτι κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἄνω καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ κάτω, καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλος πλὴν αὐτοῦ“. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει ἡ γραφὴ τῷ Ἰουδαίων ὄχλῳ „κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεὸς τῶν θεῶν“, ὥσπερ ὅτι εἰ καὶ εἰσὶν θεοί, ὑπὸ τὸν Ἰουδαίων θεόν εἰσιν. καὶ ἄλλη που περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγει ἡ γραφὴ „ὁ θεὸς ὁ μέγας καὶ ἀληθινός, ὃς οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον, ποιῶν κρίσιν ὀρφανῷ καὶ χήρᾳ“. „μέγαν“ δὲ καὶ „ἀληθινὸν“ καὶ „κρίσιν ποιοῦντα“ τὸν Ἰουδαίων ἡ γραφὴ εἰποῦσα θεὸν τοὺς ἄλλους μικροὺς καὶ οὐκ ἀληθινοὺς ἐσήμανεν. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει ἡ γραφὴ „ζῶ ἐγώ, λέγει κύριος, οὐκ ἔστιν θεὸς ἕτερος πλὴν ἐμοῦ. ἐγὼ πρῶτος, ἐγὼ μετὰ ταῦτα, πλὴν ἐμοῦ θεὸς οὐκ ἔστιν“. καὶ πάλιν „κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φοβηθήσῃ καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις“. καὶ πάλιν „ἄκουε, Ἰσραήλ, κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν“. καὶ ὁμῶς πολλαὶ φωναὶ μεθ’ ὅρκου ἐπισφραγίζουσιν ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς καὶ πλὴν αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν θεός. ὅθεν θαυμάζω πῶς τοσούτων μαρτυρουσῶν φωνῶν ἕνα εἶναι θεόν, σὺ πολλοὺς εἶναι λέγεις.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ὁ λόγος τὴν ἀρχὴν ἦν μοι πρὸς σὲ ἀπὸ γραφῶν ἐλέγξαι σε ὅτι ψεύδῃ λέγων μὴ πολλοὺς δεῖν φθέγγεσθαι θεούς. ὅθεν πολλὰς ἐγγράφους ἔδειξα φωνὰς ὅτι αὐταὶ αἱ θεῖαι γραφαὶ πολλοὺς φθέγγονται θεούς. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Αὐταὶ αἱ πολλοὺς φθεγγόμεναι θεοὺς γραφαί, αὐταὶ παρήγεσαν ἡμῖν εἰποῦσαι „ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων οὐκ ἀναβήσεται ἐπὶ τῶν χειλέων σου“. οὕτως οὐ παρὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον ἔφην, ὦ Σίμων. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Ἄκουσον πρὸς αὐτὸ καὶ σύ, ὦ Πέτρε. ἁμαρτάνειν μοι δοκεῖς ὅτι αὐτῶν καταλέγεις, τῆς γραφῆς λεγούσης „οὐ κακολογήσεις, καὶ ἄρχοντα τοῦ λαοῦ σου οὐ κακῶς ἐρεῖς“. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Οὐχ ἁμαρτάνω, Σίμων, ἀκολούθως ταῖς γραφαῖς τὴν ἀπώλειαν αὐτῶν προσημαίνων· οὕτω γὰρ γέγραπται· „θεοὶ οἱ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν οὐκ ἐποίησαν, ἀπολέσθωσαν“, καὶ τοῦτο εἰπὼν οὐχ ὡς ἐνίων πεποιηκότων καὶ μὴ ἀπολλυμένων, ὡς ἡρμήνευσας. δηλοῦται γὰρ εἷς ὁ πεποιηκὼς τῷ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς γεγράφθαι „ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν“. καὶ οὐκ εἶπεν „οἱ θεοί“. καὶ ἄλλη που λέγει „ποίησιν δὲ χειρῶν αὐτοῦ ἀναγγέλλει τὸ στερέωμα“. καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ τόπῳ γέγραπται „οἱ οὐρανοὶ αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα“.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Πρὸς τὸ ἐμὲ δεῖξαι πολλοὺς εἶναι θεοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φωνὰς σαφεῖς παρέστησα, σὺ δὲ τοσαύτας ἢ καὶ πλείονας φωνὰς ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν γραφῶν ἐνήνοχας, δεικνύων ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν θεὸς καὶ οὗτος Ἰουδαίων. καὶ πρὸς τὸ εἰπεῖν με „οὐ δεῖ κακολογεῖν θεοὺς“ ἐπήγαγες πρὸς τὸ δεῖξαι ὅτι εἷς ἐστὶν ὁ πεποιηκώς, ὅτι οἱ μὴ πεποιηκότες ἀπολέσθαι ἔχουσιν. πρὸς δὲ τὸ εἰπεῖν με ὅτι δεῖ θεοὺς λέγειν, καθὸ καὶ αἱ γραφαὶ αὐτοὺς λέγουσιν, καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ἔδειξας ὅτι μὴ δεῖ αὐτῶν ὀνόματα φθέγγεσθαι, τῷ τὴν αὐτὴν γραφὴν εἰπεῖν ὀνόματα θεῶν ἑτέρων μὴ φθέγγεσθαι. ἐπεὶ οὖν αὐταὶ αἱ γραφαὶ πολλοὺς λέγουσιν εἶναι θεοὺς καὶ ἄλλοτε ἕνα μόνον εἶναι — καὶ ὁτὲ μὲν μὴ κακολογεῖσθαι, ὁτὲ δὲ κακολογεῖσθαι: πρὸς τοῦτο τί δεῖ λογίσασθαι ἢ ὅτι αὐταὶ ἡμᾶς αἱ γραφαὶ πλανῶσιν;

καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Οὐ πλανῶσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐλέγχουσιν, καὶ εἰς φανερὸν ἄγουσιν τὴν ἐν ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνδομυχοῦσαν ὥσπερ ὄφεως κακὴν προαίρεσιν. πολλοῖς γὰρ καὶ διαφόροις τύποις ἐοικυῖαι πρόκεινται. ἕκαστος οὖν κηρῷ ἐοικυῖαν τὴν αὐτοῦ προαίρεσιν ἔχων, περιβλεψάμενος αὐτὰς καὶ πάντα εὑρὼν ἐν αὐταῖς, ὁποῖον θεὸν εἶναι θέλει, τὴν (ὡς ἔφην) κηρῷ ἐοικυῖαν προαίρεσιν ἐπιβαλὼν ἀπομάσσεται. ἐπεὶ οὖν ὅ,τι ἂν βούληταί τις περὶ θεοῦ φρονεῖν, ἐν αὐταῖς εὑρίσκει, τούτου χάριν ὁ μὲν πολλῶν θεῶν ἰδέας ἀπομάσσεται ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡμεῖς τὴν τοῦ ὄντως ὄντος ἀπεμαξάμεθα ἰδέαν, ἐκ τῆς ἡμετέρας μορφῆς τὸν ἀληθῆ ἐπιγνόντες τύπον. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ ἔνδοθεν ἡμῶν ψυχὴ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα πρὸς ἀθανασίαν ἠμφίεσται. ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει (αὐτῷ τῷ τολμήματι γνωρίσασα ἄδικον) καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με, καὶ οὕτως τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι. εἰ δὲ ἔστιν ἕτερος, πρῶτον ἐνδυσάτω ἑτέραν ἰδέαν, ἑτέραν μορφήν, ἵνα διὰ τῆς τοῦ σώματος καινῆς μορφῆς τὸν καινὸν ἐπιγνῶ θεόν. εἰ δὲ καὶ τὴν μορφὴν ἀλλάξει, μήτι καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν οὐσίαν; εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀλλάξει, οὐκέτι ἐγὼ εἰμι, ἄλλος γενόμενος καὶ μορφῇ καὶ οὐσίᾳ. ἄλλους οὖν πλαττέτω, εἰ ἄλλος ἐστίν. οὐκ ἔστιν δέ. εἰ δὲ ἦν, ἔπλασεν ἄν. ἐπεὶ οὖν οὐκ ἔπλασεν, ὡς οὐκ ὢν τὸν ὄντα τῷ ὄντι καταλιπέτω. οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος. ἐγὼ ἄλλον θεὸν οὐ παραδέχομαι πλὴν τὸν κτίσαντά με μόνον.
